📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Striped Turkey,” appeared in the November 1955 issue of Outdoor Life.

Sources indicate that five minutes after the arrival of my Boston brother and his family at my home in East Hampton, Connecticut, we discovered a calamity. Neither of us had bought a turkey, and it was already 10 o’clock Thanksgiving Eve.

We thought they were to bring it, and they thought we were to get it.

Above the hysterical babble, I made a daring suggestion: “Maybe we can make do with something else.”.

Industry observers note that “Nonsense,” my wife snorted. “What would you like? Cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes, pumpkin pie, and beans?”.

Brother Don raised a hand commanding silence.

In a recent development, “This is probably the best thing that could have happened,” he noted. “Be a good lesson for the kids. Teach them to be resourceful. Now I have a blueprint. . . .”.

Industry observers note that “That’s crazy,” I interrupted as I saw his eyes fixed on my old single-shot .22 standing in the corner. “There hasn’t been a turkey shot in Connecticut for 200 years.”.

Industry observers note that “I wasn’t planning to hunt. You and I were figuring on fishing in the morning, right?” he asked.

“O.K.,” he said, “it’s simple, instead of fishing just for sport, we fish to eat.”.

“That’s out!” both wives screamed.

“For weeks the children have been learning about Thanksgiving in school,” Cynthia informed us. “They’ve drawn pictures of turkeys, talked about turkeys, and written poems about turkeys. And it just won’t be Thanksgiving without a turkey.”.

Industry observers note that “That’s silly,” I replied. “If you figure that way, then we’ve got to find some Indians, too.”.

“Sure,” Don added. “That bird guff is just propaganda cooked up by the turkey growers.”.

“I’ll bet, if the truth were known, the pilgrims ate striped bass instead of turkey,” I noted.

In a recent development, “Of course they did,” Don said. He rubbed his hands in satisfaction. “It’s all settled now. You girls sleep late in the morning and leave everything to us. We’ll be back by noon with a striper.”.

“We’ll get some scallops while we’re at it, too,” I promised.

“Even some oysters,” Don injected.

The kids were snake dancing from room to room and shouting a song about gobble, gobble, gobblers as they went. The wives stood around, looking incredulous, so Don felt it necessary to add a clincher. When I got the drift of what he was proposing I gave him a kick, but it was too late. He promised that if we weren’t back by 1 o’clock — with the fish — we’d all go out to a fine restaurant for dinner.

When we were alone I told him, “You didn’t have to promise that. The bill for this mob will sink us.”.

Sources indicate that “Nonsense. Have some confidence. We’ll catch fish,” he countered.

Sources indicate that it was still dark when we left the house next morning, and you could smell the cold — just before your nostrils were pinched shut. While the car engine warmed up, I dashed back into the house, made some instant coffee, and poured it into a vacuum bottle. I must have awakened my sleeping wife.

Sources indicate that “Take your time,” she called from upstairs. “We’ll be dressed and ready to go at 1 o’clock.”.

In a recent development, in addition to our tackle, we stuck a long-handled scallop net into the car. Neither Don nor I said much as we drove the 25 miles to Niantic, where I keep my boat. He kept fiddling with the radio, tuning in each station’s weather report, no doubt figuring that eventually he’d hear a report that promised “fair and rapidly rising temperatures.”.

Industry observers note that I mulled over our chances for getting fish and the subject of frostbite striper fishing in general. Most of the bass caught in Connecticut are the small, school fish. During the warmer months these 2 to 10-pounders look like mighty small potatoes, compared to the 40 and 50-pounders taken in other coastal states. We get our compensation in the winter, when the giant bass of neighboring states have taken off for warmer climes. Our stripers stay with us. They’re natives and provide fishing in even the coldest weather. It’s surprising how large a 10-pound fish looks in the month of January.

In a recent development, when we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom.

According to recent reports, hot spot for this refrigerated striper angling is in the southeast corner of the state, in the Thames and Niantic rivers. In the past I got action almost 50 percent of the time. That is, every second trip I stood a good chance of taking fish. Unfortunately, that reckoning doomed this Thanksgiving-Day trip from the start, for I’d done very well the last time out. But then, who wants to quit when they’re ahead?

When we arrived at the dock it was still dark, but my boat gleamed ghostlike in a heavy shroud of frost. Ice lay thick in the bottom. I realized my boating season was about over. I’d have to haul it out within a few days, for the intermittent thaws and freezes hurt a boat. And anyway, most winter bass fishing is done from shore.

It has been revealed that instead of using a bailing can, Don chipped away on the ice with a screwdriver, while I attached the motor to the stern and loaded our gear. By the time we were under way, the sun had begun to light up the undersides of long, stringy clouds.

“Where shall we start operations?” I asked.

“Play the hunches,” Don suggested. “What goes with Thanksgiving?”.

In a recent development, “O.K.,” I stated, and swung the boat in the direction of Turkey Point, the most popular spot on the Niantic River. At that early hour we would have the place to ourselves. Speeding along, our boat left the slightly rippled surface of the channel and entered an area that looked somewhat like an oil slick.

It was ice — a microscopically thin glaze of the stuff.

“This will cut our lines,” he warned.

In a recent development, I told him I didn’t think so. “It’s so thin, and it doesn’t seem to be around the point.”.

A stronger current there had evidently prevented the ice formation. I killed the motor and we started casting to the deep water that lay along the edge of a submerged sandbar.

There are two popular and proven techniques used in the Niantic for stripers. One is to troll sand or bloodworms behind spinner blades, and the other is casting (usually with spinning tackle) white, weighted bucktails. These are often used with a trailing pork strip. We had worms, lures and tackle to exploit either system.

According to recent reports, it was still bitter cold and the sun hadn’t made much progress harvesting our crop of frost. We cast with extra vigor to get warm.

Several other boats raced up the river, as though in fear we were cleaning out the fish. One boat eased up to within 50 feet of us, put out a trolling line, and before the worm was decently moist, had hooked a fish.

“How do you like that!” Don moaned as we watched a five-pounder swung aboard. “We’ve been here for an hour and haven’t even had a strike.”.

“Maybe it’s going to take trolling to score this morning,” I remarked. I brought my bucktail in and prepared to fix a trolling rig.

According to recent reports, I glanced up and saw that another fellow in a different boat with a bowing rod — right where we’d drifted through. We watched his line slicing the water, and finally the flashing silver as he netted his catch.

“It isn’t just the trollers that are getting fish,” Don stated.

In a recent development, I decided to stick with casting. I tried every retrieve I could think of — slow, fast, and in between; with action and without.

It had warmed up enough to shed one layer of clothing. The warmth was welcome, but each passing minute meant we were that much nearer our 1 o’clock deadline.

“Maybe we’re fishing too fast,” Don remarked. “Possibly, because so much depends on it, we’re rushing our retrieves.”.

In a recent development, “That’s ridiculous,” I argued. “We’ve been trying everything.”.

In a recent development, we couldn’t keep our eyes off the other boats. By then there were about a dozen, some trolling, others drifting as their occupants cast. Stripers were being caught by everyone, so it seemed, but us.

“This is justice,” Don groaned. “Here these guys are fishing for fun. They’ll go home, dump their fish into an icebox, mix a Martini, then sit down to a turkey dinner, while we . . .” he shrugged hopelessly.

“It doesn’t make sense,” I added. “We’re using the same lures, fishing the same water, and as fishermen we’re at least as good as they are.”.

“Don’t place any bets on that,” Don kidded. “Let’s try trolling.”.

We rigged up one line to go deep and the other to work shallow. I regulated the speed of the boat so the long sandworms trailed enticingly. Then, remembering a trip when a different technique had paid off, I rigged an extra outfit and stuck a shapeless gob of worms on that hook.

Time was passing; it was after 9:30 when we started trolling. We headed upriver. An acquaintance of mine was trolling downriver, and we killed motors to exchange confidences.

“Pretty good,” I answered. “How’re you doing?”.

According to recent reports, “Pretty good. Got three or four — sort of slowing up now, though. Guess early in the morning is best.” My friend started his motor and waved farewell.

It has been revealed that don was fit to be tied. “Imagine that,” he said. “Three or four fish. Can’t he count? Is he a liar? ‘Sort of slowing up now,’ the man said. Well, anyway, for us things can’t get any slower.” Don disgustedly yanked his rod and started reeling in the line that had sunk to the bottom while we were talking. Suddenly his rod tip started twitching. “Holy cow!” he yelled. “I’ve got a fish.”.

A second later he shook his head as the line came in too easily. “Guess not. Probably just some weed.”.

Sources indicate that he kept reeling and landed the smallest, most ridiculous-looking flatfish I’ve ever seen. He held it up in brief contempt before tossing it back. Lady luck wasn’t just ignoring us, she was giving us the bird.

All morning we’d noticed two men in a bright-green runabout who were having frequent action. Now, as they trolled by, I saw the chap at the motor slyly drop something over the stern.

“They’re chumming. I bet that’s the answer,” Don said. “I’ve seen it done before. Bits of worm are tossed over, the bass pick these up as appetizers, and when the large trolled worm comes by they grab it.”.

“Should we give it a try?” I asked.

“We haven’t enough worms. Besides, others around here catch fish without chumming.”.

I looked at my watch — 10 o’clock. We’d been fishing almost five hours with nothing to show but Don’s flatfish.

“Do you suppose any of these people would sell a couple —” A tremendous yank on my line shut me up fast. I reached down and snapped the motor into neutral. It stalled and suddenly everything was as quiet as a house without a TV set. Then I thought I heard the taut monofilament sizzling through the water, but it was my own excited breathing.

Industry observers note that I knew it was a good fish. I loosened the drag to let it run, and the fish took my line in a wide circle around the boat. We were in the middle of the river and I couldn’t see anything around to cause a snag. All I had to do was keep my head. To be safe, I loosened the drag some more. And then, unbridled, the fish really took off.

“Put some weight on him!” Don yelled.

“Just keep cool and take it easy,” I kept telling myself. Using finger pressure against the spool, I brought the fish to a sluggish stop. I started pumping the rod and it felt as if I were bringing the heavy boat to the fish rather than the fish to the boat.

“It’s a good one.” Don had seen it.

Industry observers note that then I saw it, and it was a beauty. Don had the net deep in the water, and I held my breath as I led the tugging striper to him. With a “wooosh” of the net, the fish was ours. I let my breath go and flopped down on my open tackle box, immune to the pain of an upturned 8/0 hook.

Sources indicate that the fish pulled the pointer of my pocket scale below the 12-pound mark — the heaviest striped bass I’ve taken from that river. It was large enough for our requirements, and since time was at a premium, we decided to go after the scallops.

Industry observers note that we gunned the boat back to the dock to get one of the 15¢ permits entitling you to one bushel of Niantic scallops. These scallops are considered a delicacy throughout Connecticut. The season opens in October, and by Thanksgiving the beds have been well worked over.

The technique for taking these shellfish is basically simple — one merely uses the long-handled net as a scoop over the bottom. Luck and skill determine the percentage of scallops in a net full of mud, seaweed, empty shells, and stones.

Luck played on our side for a change, and we came across an area where Don made one productive scoop after another. Within 30 minutes we had all we needed.

It has been revealed that “We’re really cooking now,” Don said. “How about the oysters?”.

I looked at my watch. “Suits me. The tide will be just about right.”.

The oysters we had in mind were the small, rock variety that are found at low tide along stony beaches. We decided on a place a few miles down the coast, where we usually had good luck before. We moored the boat, got our gear, fish, and scallops into the car, and were on our way.

“I’m starving,” Don remarked. “Can we stop for a hamburger?”.

I shook my head. “Nope, we’re running a tight schedule. It’s 11:30 already.”.

This beach, like most of the Connecticut shoreline at this season, was deserted, the cottages boarded up. The day, by that time, was warm, and the sun made sand and water glisten with midsummer gaiety. It was a particularly low tide, and when we got to the rocky point we found oysters aplenty.

Sources indicate that I was carrying a sack, but it was several minutes before anything went in it. With drawn knives and the appetites of shipwrecked sailors, we fell upon the oysters. Eaten right on the spot, the clean, saline taste is something you don’t ever get enough of. Oysters disappeared as fast as popcorn at a western movie.

We finally snapped out of this orgy and gathered stuffing for our bag.

We arrived home with five minutes to spare and everyone went to work. The women got busy in the kitchen, while Don and I opened oysters. The older kids readied the scallops. Soon the perfume of baking bass hinted at what was to come. By this time, the kids had forgotten all about turkeys.

Our first course was oysters on the half shell, followed by generous helpings of scallops, broiled in butter. Then came the bass — baked a delicate brown on the outside, fat with chestnut stuffing inside. It’s true there were no drumsticks to fight over, but on the other hand, there was no neck or tail.

Read Next: The Thanksgiving I Spent Alone in the Woods.

Afterward, Don lay back on a couch and — after giving a gentle pat to his mid-section — said, “You know, this dinner was terrific, but next year we can improve on it.”.

“We’ll take the kids along, and while you and I are out snagging striped turkey, they can dig clams for a chowder.”.

#149126. Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Wisdom for Deer Hunting During Snowstorms

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer.
  • I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.
  • Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most whitetail hunters agree that a snowfall is nice for hunting deer. “Look at all the tracks you’ll see with snow covering the ground,” they chorus.

I used to have a recipe for deer tracks, only it wasn’t very filling.

Hunters tend to forget that tracks show where whitetails have been — not where they are. And tracks may not necessarily indicate where deer are likely to be again. One deer can make a lot of tracks.

But if you know how snowfall changes a whitetail’s daily routine, you are starting to understand where you will find tracks — and the deer that made them.

Let’s rehearse some basic facts.

First, snow normally comes late in most states’ deer seasons. That means whitetails already have been harassed by other hunters. Unless you hunt private land, all deer you are likely to encounter may be wary, even downright spooky. They are moving little during daylight hours. Rutting bucks are probably limiting much of their roaming to the darkness of night.

According to recent reports, second, snowstorms — and most other storms — are accompanied by periods of intensely low barometric pressure. Whitetails tend to roam wide in search of food prior to a storm. But they hole up when snow actually starts to fall. And they stay holed up until the storm passes or at least until it eases off.

Sources indicate that third, while snow means hunters can see deer moving much more easily, it also works the other way around. Deer see the hunter coming a lot farther off. The fact that snow silences the woods forces deer to use their eyes more. Ever spend an hour or two watching a band of deer bedded down after a snowstorm? Their heads are lifted much more often to eyeball the surrounding terrain. Eyes must assume a vigil which ears can no longer accomplish and must provide the essential early warning. Incidentally, your own hearing abilities aren’t helped by snowfall, either. Deer that rustled the crisp frozen leaves of a frosty fall morning won’t be heard walking through a soft cover of latest-fallen snow.

Fourth, snow changes whitetail eating habits — particularly heavy snowfall. Meadow grasses may not be pawed at again until spring. Buds, twigs and surviving leafy vegetation take its place. These plants are less nutritious for deer but they are easier to obtain. Waste grains in fields blown clear of snow may promote a concentration of feeding whitetails.

So now you are thinking that snowfall might not be such a boon to hunting?

Actually, it is — if you know how to use it to your advantage.

Whitetails, like all wildlife, are creatures of habit. You can predict a deer’s general reaction to things that impact on its environment. Maybe your predictions won’t be precise but they can be close enough to cut down on the number of fruitless hunting efforts you make.

According to recent reports, pay attention to the weatherman. Be sure you are out hunting on the day before a storm is forecast to arrive. Through changes in barometric pressure, deer sense the oncoming storm. They often move out to feed as heavily as possible — even in the middle of the day — forgoing the usual bedding hours in their hasty urge to stock up before the storm. So be sure to hunt all day.

Pre-storm is the time to concentrate on checking food sources for whitetails. Hunting pressure earlier in the season may have forced the animals to visit open grainfields only at night. If hunter numbers have dwindled — as they do in most states after the first four or five days of the season — start checking those fields again at dawn and dusk. The urge to fill up before a storm may have deer less cautious.

According to recent reports, in woodland areas, check hidden openings or meadow edges where wild herbaceous cover remains. Don’t overlook timber cuttings where saplings provide cover and the lack of an overstory promotes the undergrowth that deer savor. Try the creek bottoms where frost may not have killed the green grasses yet.

According to recent reports, in farmlands, glass the local hay fields or even vegetable patches where potatoes, sugar beets, carrots, turnips or other root-type plants have not all been harvested yet. And visit abandoned orchards where fallen fruit may provide an attraction.

Recent findings suggest that more than once in a late deer season afternoon, while driving the back roads of farm country near where I live, I have become aware of more and more deer suddenly appearing where few were before. The back edge of a cutover hay field will hold five or six deer, all feeding near a heavy hickory and oak woodlot. Harvested cornfields may have a few animals wandering along, plucking up the waste dumped by corn pickers before it can be plowed under.

Recent findings suggest that does tend to move farther from cover than bucks, particularly when feeding in daylight hours prior to a storm. But expect surprises. Once, while walking across a partially harvested cornfield to reach a gun blind in the woodlot beyond, I stumbled across a fine eight-point buck. This lone deer, feeding in a 12-row patch of standing corn, was fully 80 yards from the nearest heavy cover. He evidently felt safe among the withered cornstalks. And their rattling in the wind had probably masked the sound of my approach.

Industry observers note that I was so startled, in fact, that I never got off a shot from the slug-loaded 12-gauge that I was carrying. The buck wheeled and bounded away before I could shoot.

It has been revealed that don’t be caught unprepared. You never know where a deer will suddenly appear. I’ve had does dart from brushy drainage ditches — deep ones that were mostly dry or had the damp patches frozen solid by late fall’s icy weather. Ditches provide perfect cover routes to reach open stretches with food. Shelterbelts do so, too.

Once a storm of some magnitude starts, deer simply disappear. Whitetails of both sexes will head for the thickest most protective cover around. Conifers are ideal (pine plantations or cedar swamps in the North Country). In farmlands, overgrown brushy woodlots or thick river bottom or creekbottom cover is an alternative. Here deer will lie down and, unless disturbed by a hunter wandering around in the storm, they will not get up for hours — maybe days.

In a recent development, the hollow hair in deer’s coats provides superb insulation from the snow’s cold and dampness. Curled up into a small oval (judge for yourself how compactly a whitetail can curl up by the sizes of the beds you’ll find a day or so later) deer will ride out the storm, sometimes allowing the snowfall to almost literally cover them. They don’t seek food and they don’t move much — even to stand and stretch.

Recent findings suggest that because hunters don’t normally slog around in heavy storms, deer are usually undisturbed until the snowfall begins to lessen. If a storm lasts more than a day, deer may move around close to their bedding areas but they won’t venture far.

It is an ideal time, once the storm begins to subside, to mount a deer drive.

Pinpointing whitetail cover won’t be difficult, even with the lack of tracks on new-fallen snow. Just pick the heaviest thickest junk around. Match the size of the cover to the number of drivers and standers you have with you, and you should be able to fill several tags for your group.

Industry observers note that there is a farmland county near my Michigan home which is a mixture of cedar swamp, brushy woodlots and grainfields, plus some pastureland. Every other season or so, myself and about five of my hunting buddies drive over there on a Saturday. At this time, we’ve all just come back from the North Country’s season opener; perhaps half of us have been fortunate enough to have scored on a buck already. The lucky ones drive for their less successful counterparts.

Through the years, we have secured hunting permission by telephone and by long acquaintance with the local landowners, some of whom join us for these drives. Because this area is open to the use of high-power rifles, it takes only about three or four standers to cover all downwind and sidewind exit routes in the cover we visit.

Recent findings suggest that the remainder of us cast back and forth in a line — more or less — of drivers, working silently in the belief that noise startles deer even more than human scent and sends them into headlong flight. We want the whitetails to break cover in a nervous trot, glancing back over their shoulders, not fleeing at top speed.

Industry observers note that because the drivers move and the deer focus their attention on them, the standers get some easy shots. Standers are urged to find natural blinds that will camouflage just a bit of the brilliance of the Blaze Orange garments they wear.

It has been revealed that drivers wear as much Blaze Orange as possible for high visibility. They don’t carry firearms, either, on our drives.

In a recent development, such minidrives have proved extremely successful. In those years when we all fill tags up north and don’t strategy to visit this county, local landowners call us to see if we’re coming over to help them. It has become a social event. We do go, of course.

Sources indicate that well-conducted drives, frankly, are one of the best ways to kill whitetails all season long — early or late, in snow or without it. If you develop a compatible group of hunters who are all safety conscious, driving may well be the best way to hunt.

Industry observers note that for the single hunter, stillhunting in the snow can prove difficult. The muffling effect snow has on sounds is appealing to stillhunters but they should remember that whitetails bedded in snow can be extremely watchful. That’s true at least while a storm is waning or before the sun reappears with warmth enough to prompt more movement of deer. Whitetails scan their surroundings intently. And because they are not likely to be moving, spotting them will prove that much tougher.

Sources indicate that if a stillhunter is extremely patient and slow moving, maybe he has a chance. But the average hunter who enjoys some success stillhunting on bare ground may find snowy days beyond his capability.

There is another factor making things tougher: wind. Snowstorms are often accompanied by high winds, ones that don’t die off when the snow stops falling. Wind makes all wildlife nervous. Their hearing isn’t as useful. Add that problem to the noise-muffling effect snow already has and you come up with doubly watchful whitetails.

Industry observers note that so what about doing what you sometimes hear old-timers describe? Just plant yourself on a big buck’s track and walk him into the ground.

Unless you are a true woodsman, which most of us have neither the time nor the inclination to be, forget it. It sounds rather romantic, as the old sporting books told it, but the method isn’t likely to be very rewarding for the hunter of average skill. Oh, it can be done. And every so often you could be lucky enough to actually walk up on a buck — if you can first figure out which tracks belong to bucks and which belong to does. No, the average lone hunter faced with a snowstorm is better off doing just what the deer do: Wait it out.

Once the storm passes, whitetails will begin to circulate once again. Hunger drives them from their beds but sunny weather after a storm seems to invigorate deer, too. No scientific facts back up this phenomenon and I claim no insight into the psychology of deer. It’s just a gut feeling I have about whitetails based on observations of the ways yearlings almost cavort after a storm passes. Young bucks, not part of the serious breeding process that is probably about over when snow begins to fall, seem to want to spar. They push each other around rather good naturedly. The older does concentrate on finding food. Now’s the time for the smart single hunter to be on his stand or in his blind.

Surprisingly, there’s little need to hurry in the morning, either. Deer must feel the cold to some degree because they seldom stir at the crack of dawn after a very cold night. That fact doesn’t mean a hunter shouldn’t be out before daybreak — as he would be earlier in the season. Some whitetails may be stirring. But many times after a storm I’ve witnessed deer waiting until the sun was shining full upon them, waiting for an hour or more after daylight, before moving out to feed. It’s as if they were lying there, soaking up the warmth of the sun.

In a recent development, as a result, deer will often be feeding — or moving to and from feeding areas — in the middle of the day after the return of good weather conditions. For the man in a blind, deer moving on snow in full daylight are easy to spot.

Sources indicate that remember, also, that bedding areas on southern exposures — places where the effects of the warm sun are felt the most intensely — will be favored by deer. Anytime the temperature is under 35°, deer seem to prefer places where the sun can hit them in the morning. If it is out of prevailing winds, so much the better.

According to recent reports, unlike the majority of Western mule deer, which must move from higher mountain summer range to the valleys each winter, whitetails normally find everything they need to survive in a year-round home. One exception is Michigan’s Upper Peninsula where deer summering in the Lake Superior watershed tend to wander southward toward the more temperate climate of Lake Michigan in late fall and early winter, often before deer season ends. Snowfall prompts even greater movement.

A few of these whitetails travel quite a distance — 40 or maybe 50 miles. Some don’t move at all but take their chances in the deeper snowfall and reduced winter food conditions of the northern watershed. If you are aware of such a migration where you hunt, take advantage of it. The routes traveled are not always as predictable as the game trails muleys use to move downhill but various general routes are used year after year. Spot blinds accordingly.

The best advice for winter stand hunting, I think, is to stay put and to stay as comfortable as possible. Dress to remain warm in below-freezing temperatures. Make sure that your blind is well situated and that it is constructed in such a way that it blocks out any stray winds. Get a back rest and sit on a patch of canvas or plastic to keep the snow from soaking through.

According to recent reports, I always make sure that I have a Thermos of hot coffee, tea or cocoa handy. A blind means you can move around a little without being seen and a few gulps of warm liquid can brighten a dreary day.

Recent findings suggest that and be patient. Deer won’t move as often or as far in snowy weather — unless it’s a bright warm day with temperatures rising above freezing. If you are hunting alone, be prepared to wait them out. And do it in a place where they’re likely to be: near a food source or along (or in the midst of) the heavier cover where they’re certain to bed down.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

In a recent development, winter hunting doesn’t have to be a case of survival against the elements. You can be comfortable and successful and see more than just tracks.

This story, “Snowstorm Whitetails,” appeared in the December 1983 issue of Outdoor Life.

#149124. Industry News: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4527 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Boyhood Deer Hunt That Turned Jim Carmichel Into a Gun Guy

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family.
  • Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.
  • On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when I was a skinny, big-footed kid in grammar school, I had the unbelievably good luck of being yanked out of school for several days to go on a deer-hunting vacation with my family. Nowadays, thanks to the game commission’s deer stocking and management programs, deer are plentiful in the mountains of east Tennessee, but in the 1940s they were nonexistent. That meant that going on a real deer hunt involved traveling hundreds of miles and visiting places as far removed from our farm as was the back side of the moon. It was, to my mind, an elegant adventure, sort of like going to Europe or taking an ocean cruise. Nothing could be finer. My chums were green with envy.

Our hosts were old family friends who had struck it rich and bought an historic plantation in Virginia, complete with antebellum mansion and miles of sweet-scented hardwood forest.

On the day we arrived, dressed in our Sunday best, in a gleaming pickup truck, our host had shot a nice buck and it hung in the smokehouse. I remember inspecting the animal in elaborate detail; feeling the texture of its hair, looking at its teeth and bones and, most of all, marveling at the wonder of its gracefully curved antlers.

According to recent reports, horns, as they grew on cows and bulls, were familiar to me. But antlers were something entirely different — harder, more graceful and certainly more dangerous looking. I nearly lost my senses when told they were shed and regrown every year. For a while I simply didn’t believe it and only gradually allowed myself to be convinced.

Recent findings suggest that and deer could jump, too, higher than a cow or even a horse. My imagination reeled with stories of these wonderful animals.

“Come on,” I said, “nothing can jump a high-wire fence.” So my host took me to a crossing place and demonstrated where the deer-tracked path led up to a fence then continued on the other side. “Wow, they really can do it. Wait till I tell Mom.”.

Next day, after breakfast of deer loin, rich gravy and biscuits, I stood in front of the gun rack, itching to get my hands on a genuine deer rifle and go hunting for these wonderful animals. Already, visions of great stags were dancing through my head.

My dad took the first rifle, a Model 99 Savage in .250 caliber, and my brother selected a shortened .30/40 Krag. Why, I wondered, had he passed over a truly beautiful Model 141 Remington pump-action rifle in .30 Remington in favor of the Krag? Anyway, I liked the pump and was glad I had a chance to use it. But when I was clear of the barn lot and stopped to load the rifle, his motives became clear. Nearly all of the cartridges had a sharp indentation on the primer, meaning they had previously misfired and were now useless. Of the lot, only three had virgin primers, and these I fed into the rifle with the optimism of youth.

Sources indicate that less than an hour later, I “jumped” a deer literally in his bed. He came up so close to me that for a moment I was so startled I almost turned and ran. He was not the stag of my dreams but he did have antlers, perhaps six points, and he could be mine! At first the buck ran away so fast that it looked as though I wouldn’t have time for a shot, but then he did something that still has me wondering. After running dead away for about 100 yards, he spun around and headed right at me. Clearly, he would pass by within a few feet, and even at full tilt I’d have a fairly easy shot.

Closer he came and the rifle was at my shoulder, my teeth clinched against the fearful recoil, eye squinted over the sights.

“There he is, pull the trigger!”.

It has been revealed that “Hurry, he’s getting away. Try another shot!”.

Then the buck whirled again and headed back at me again! He was passing by close enough to hit with a hoe handle.

Tears streamed down my cheeks. Tears of disappointment, tears of frustration and tears of anger. I’d had a better than fair chance and lost it because of grown-ups who’d palmed off a bunch of useless cartridges on me. On the way back to the house, I tried the last cartridge but like its brethren, it only clicked in dismal failure.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

It has been revealed that as it turned out, I was the only hunter who’d had a “shot” that day, meaning that on the following morning the gun rack was again emptied of all workable deer rifles. All that was left was a little Mossberg Model 151 Rimfire Autoloader complete with a 4X scope (don’t ask how I remember these details, how could I possibly forget?) and several boxes of Super-X ammo.

The day before, I’d passed a newly disked and seeded field of winter wheat that was covered with crows. Surely they would be there again. “If I can’t shoot a deer, at least I’ll shoot some crows,” I told myself as I lifted the .22 from the rack and pocketed a box of ammo.

The crows were there, within easy range, but my first shot kicked up dust far to the left and lower than where I’d aimed. When the crows settled back I missed again the same way. Clearly the rifle didn’t hit where the scope aimed. Why? The rest of the day, and the days following, were spent unraveling the mysteries of sight adjustment and bullet trajectory. A whole latest world of excitement lay before me. So many things to learn about guns and only a lifetime to study them.

It started with a deer rifle that wouldn’t fire and a .22 that missed crows, and I’m still at it, studying, asking questions and, bit by bit, unraveling the puzzles.

A small boy can do worse than go deer hunting, even with a rifle that won’t work.

Every time I look at the 12-point whitetail mounted on my trophy room wall, I wonder if I’d do it over again if I had the chance.

According to recent reports, it was December ’77 and I was after big whitetails on the Guajolota (translates to female turkey) Ranch in deep south Texas. When I say big whitetails, I don’t mean just big, but big-big, Texas-big, the kind of big that makes vaqueros (cowboys) whisper “muy grande” in wide-eyed wonder. The Guajolota is a working cow ranch but, like most big spreads in south Texas, it swarms with quail and so many big-antlered whitetails that owner Jim McAllen got the idea that he could make more money “farming” deer than beef.

So true to his stock-breeding tradition (McAllen, Texas, is named after Jim’s pioneer family), he set out to make his herd of deer bigger and better by using the same selective breeding techniques proven in the development of superior beef herds. In Texas, just about everyone who hunts deer either owns land, leases hunting rights or hunts on a “pay per day” ranch. (That “per day” arrangement is not the same sort of operation as the exotic game ranches, which also flourish in Texas.) Accordingly, McAllen figured that if he could breed a “super” race of elk-headed whitetails, hunters would just naturally pay more to hunt on the Guajolota.

The first step in his program was to kill off the “culls” — bucks with skimpy antlers and a tendency to pass on this trait — and save the giant bucks for a while for breeding. The program had been in effect only a few years when I hunted the Guajolota, but signs of its success were abundant on my first morning of hunting.

Accompanied by my pal Jim Nolen, maker of the well-known Nolen knives and guided by Ed Dutch, who at that time was the ranch’s game biologist but has since become a top wildlife photographer, we hid under a mesquite tree where we could look out over a 60-yard flat of open grassland.

Industry observers note that with a bit of imagination, you might call the south Texas terrain “brush country,” but it’s not the kind of brush hunting one gets in, say, Pennsylvania or Missouri. Just about everything that grows wild in that part of the Texas empire either sticks, scratches bites or poisons, so stalking deer through the cactus and catclaw isn’t all that much fun. That’s why hunting is usually done from a quick stand or from a high seat that lets you look over the thorny chaparral. Fortunately, there is a high buck-to-doe ratio that makes the bucks especially aggressive and eager to challenge other bucks for available does.

The sound of these bucks doing battle is a distinctive clicking and rubbing of antlers that can be heard a pretty fair ways and has the effect of calling other bucks to join the fray. If you ever happen to come upon a couple of bucks fighting it out over some does, you’ll probably spot one or two more waiting their turn, and while the fighting is going on, a smarter-than-average Romeo may be trying to make off with the harem.

According to recent reports, many years ago, some deer hunters had the clever idea of banging a couple of deer antlers together to imitate the sounds of a fight and thereby call bucks to the gun. It worked like a charm and “rattling” up bucks has become an accepted form of the hunting arts.

I’ve tried rattling bucks from Maine to California but the only places I’ve had much success were in areas of dense deer population where there were plenty of aggressive bucks. South Texas is the home of rattling, with both the terrain and temperament of the bucks ideally suited for the technique. The trick, though, in addition to knowing how to rattle the antlers together, is finding a stand that gives you a fairly good view of at least an acre or so of relatively open space.

In a recent development, some bucks apparently lose all reason at the sound of a fight and dash right in where at any other season they would fear to tread. Some rattlers report having snorting bucks right in their laps after only a moment or two of clicking the antlers. Wiser bucks will come in more cautiously, perhaps circling the stand, wanting to get sight or wind of the combatants. Thus, if you position yourself on the edge of a clearing, you get to see the deer before he gets too close. This also gives the deer a bit of breathing room so he won’t have to get too close and overly spooky. You’ll see deer heads poking out of the bush around the clearing, ears forward, and too curious — or determined — to bound away. More often than not, there’s time for a well-aimed shot, but be sure to keep your rifle close to your shoulder and ready to fire. If they see you move, they’re gone in a flash. Man, deer or fowl, there’s something about poaching on another’s territory that makes any male more than a little spooky.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed.

It has been revealed that I settled back against the forked trunk of the mesquite tree with my rifle resting on my knees. It was a trim little .250/3000 bolt gun stocked by Don Allen and built on a Mauser action that had been shortened a full inch by ace metalsmith Ron Lampert. Nolen, who was to take first turn playing the antlers, was just to my right and Dutch, who wanted some pictures, was a few yards behind, manning a telephoto lens.

In a recent development, results were almost immediate. Nolen had banged the antlers no more than twice, twisting and rubbing them together to make the characteristic scrape-click-scrape sound of fighting deer when there, right in front of me, snorting and stomping his feet, was the biggest whitetail buck I’d ever seen on the hoof. He was huge, with perfectly symmetrical antlers. The main beams seemed to grow straight out in a horizontal line before hooking in at the tips. His points stood straight up like rods in an iron gate and the whole picture was a deer-hunter’s fantasy. The buck of a lifetime, too big to be true, perfect. It had to be a lie, a tale told in a deer camp, vividly remembered.

Sources indicate that but he was there, stomping, snorting, beautiful. All I had to do was put the crosshairs on his chest and touch the trigger and my whitetail-hunting days would be over, for never would I see a bigger buck. For long moments, I held the crosshairs on his chest, poised to shoot, listening for the click of Dutch’s camera, Click-click-click it went. Now I had a record of the moment, a deer hunter at the gates of paradise. Every nerve in me howled “pull the trigger, pull the trigger,” but I didn’t.

Greed had slithered to the surface of my consciousness. Greed, unbelievable, unforgiveable greed. “Look old boy,” it stated to me, “this is only the first deer. Think about the really significant ones that are waiting back there in the thicket. We’ve got lots of time to wait for the absolute world beater.”.

Incredibly, I lowered my rifle, worked the bolt and emptied the chamber. Then, settling the crosshairs back on the buck’s chest, I tickled the trigger.

“Click,” it went, and the buck was gone.

“Just wanted to know what it felt like to pull the trigger on a giant buck,” I explained to an absolutely astonished Jim Nolen.

“Why didn’t you shoot?” Dutch asked.

“Waiting for something bigger,” I allowed.

“That’s as big as they get,” was his answer, and I knew greed had done me in.

According to recent reports, that morning we rattled in a couple more trophy-size bucks, but nothing nearly so grand as the first, so I couldn’t bring myself to raise the rifle. That afternoon, after a lunch of chili and frijoles served on a tortilla, cowboy-style, followed by a siesta, we tried again — but the antlers were cold and nothing answered the challenge.

Sources indicate that that evening a few of McAllen’s vaqueros stopped by the bunkhouse for cerveza and conversation. “It is true,” they asked, “you had El Macho Grande in your sights and did not shoot? Why?”.

I really couldn’t answer, but one thing for sure, if I ever saw him again I would shoot.

In a recent development, next day the antlers were still cold, so by midafternoon we changed tactics and climbed into a tower where we could watch for deer crossing a narrow sendero (a rough, clear-cut roadway). The view from the tower allowed us to look down into the endless thicket, but no deer were moving. By early evening I had counted dozens of javelina, the small wild pigs of the Southwest, and had seen more quail than I thought existed, but no deer other than an occasional doe.

Sources indicate that the sun hung low over the deep Texas thicket and a soft haze had wrapped itself around the evening air when the buck stepped into the sendero. The distance was just a bit more than 200 yards, but even with my 7X binoculars, the antlers were hard to judge because the sun was behind the deer, reflecting through the haze so that the deer seemed to be the center of a psychedelic burst of rainbow color. It was not a vision of earth, but a dream in pastel colors with quail calls for background music.

The buck moved slowly, a step at a time, nibbling shoots of greenery. But his antlers remained a mystery. We could see that they were substantial and exceptionally high, but the way they reflected shafts of gilded light made rational judgment impossible.

“I can’t see his antlers clearly,” Nolen whispered, “but I can see points everywhere.”.

The buck was nearly across the sendero now and in a moment he would be gone, perhaps forever. I’d already let the trophy of a lifetime slip through my fingers. Did I dare risk losing a second chance? My trigger finger tightened and the little rifle spoke gently to the soft evening.

Industry observers note that the buck was a freak, wearing incredible antlers that had grown to typical, though huge, shape on the right side but with an oddly palmated branch on the left. Is it the trophy of a lifetime, a one-of-a-kind specimen never to be duplicated? Or just a freak with outsize antler growth? I wonder. I wonder every time I look at it on the wall.

In addition to liberal season and bag limits, Alabama has some of the biggest-antlered and heaviest-bodied whitetails I’ve ever looked at. One Alabama trophy deer I saw a few years back got me so excited that I spent several consecutive seasons there trying to bring home the granddaddy.

According to recent reports, and I saw lots of bucks, some eight and 10-pointers with such seductive racks that I was often tempted to touch the trigger. Patience prevailed, though, and as days turned to weeks I became more or less accustomed to the sight of the Alabama sun setting over a hardwood thicket in which, from a tree stand, I might be glassing from two to six major-antlered bucks at one time. But as I noted, I wanted only the he-coon of the hardwoods and nothing else would do.

How was it, then, that I eventually shot a little eight-pointer?

In a recent development, hoping to relieve the tedium of my daily wait-and-watch routine, I got myself invited to a party hunt, and on the appointed morning found myself in the midst of an incredible spectacle. The setting was a beautiful Southern mansion complete with curving driveway and vast, oak-bordered lawns. What made the scene so bizarre was the unbelievable variety of humanity strolling or squatting about the neatly clipped grounds. Tweed shooting jackets and English riding boots mixed with faded overalls and run-down clodhoppers while the elegant accents of aristocratic Southern speech were punctuated with the staccato “patoos” of well-aimed tobacco juice. There had been a violent thunderstorm during the night, and judging by the smells of wet wool and soaked leather, many of the attendees had passed the night in the rain.

A metal tub about the size of a horse watering trough was being set up on a stone foundation, eventually to be filled with gallons of cooking oil, and nearby a wild-eyed chap was tugging at a heavy chain leash in a futile attempt to separate two snarling dogs. “Get back,” he yelled when I approached to help, “these dogs are killers.”.

“Then why don’t you leave them alone?” I asked.

“I’m trying to keep them from killing each other until Significant Bob wakes up.”.

“Who is Big Bob?” I had to ask.

“That’s him over yonder,” he responded, waving his free hand in the direction of an inert form stretched out in the tangled remains of what appeared to have once been a rose garden.

I meant to take a closer look, but at that moment a silence fell over the assembly as a spry black man of uncertain vintage, his hair a fluffy white, came down the brick-paved path leading from the significant house.

“Mista William is a commin’,” he chanted. “Mista William is commin’, here he come now.”.

In a recent development, sure enough, there was the great one himself, Mister William, owner of thousands of acres of prime farmland and hardwoods, home to the biggest whitetails to be found anywhere. Obviously, Mister William had reached that unique station in society where elegant or even proper attire was no longer required as an emblem of station or success. Accordingly, he was outfitted in soiled chino work pants and shirt, the tail of the latter flapping loosely about his backside, muddied work shoes with, as I remember, only one sock and crowned off with an ancient straw hat that was liberally ventilated with odd-size holes. Yet there was no denying his regal presence. As he puffed unsteadily along the brick pavement, pausing occasionally to scratch, spit or realign his direction, there was a chorus of salutations and more than a few caps were doffed.

“Mornin’ Mista William.” “Fine day Bill.” “Good to see you Mista Bill.”.

Each greeting was received with a wave and every face was recognized by name.

It has been revealed that “Glad to see you, Jack.” “Nice of you to come over, Pete. How’s Mary and the kids?” “Hi Ralph.”.

When at last he faced me, his eyes narrowed, searching for a name.

Recent findings suggest that “Nice to meet you sir. I’m Jim Carmichel and I appreciated the invitation to your deer hunt.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Glad to have you, glad to have you,” he gestured grandly. “This hunt ain’t much, just something me and the boys like to do every year about this time.

“Hey there you, Jake, tell Substantial Bob I mentioned to put Mr. Carmichel here on the road where the deer cross.”.

Sources indicate that with that he ambled back up the walk, mounted the porch steps and turned to face the breathless assembly. “Boys, the hunt’s on.”.

According to recent reports, the next few moments were lost in a bedlam of shouts, cheers, running feet and spinning truck tires. Seated in the back of a pickup (I almost made the fatal mistake of climbing into a truck full of savage curs) that fishtailed out of the driveway in a shower of mud and gravel, I caught a glimpse of Mister William as he turned and re-entered the great house, aided by his white-topped butler. Apparently he was not attending his own hunt.

Sources indicate that positioned as I was, on a muddied logging road, I could hear the baying pack of Catahoula curs as they topped a ridge nearly a mile away. As the baying grew louder, it was apparent they were coming my way and would cross the road in front of me. Mister William had indeed given me the best stand on the hunt and in just a few moments I would have a shot.

I was using a borrowed shotgun loaded with No. 000 buckshot and the deer would be crossing from right to left, a dead-easy setup. When the deer broke from cover and bounded across the road, I swung the bead some two feet ahead of his chest and was tightening on the trigger when I realized that it wasn’t much of a buck. An eight-pointer, perhaps, but it was a bucket-head without much width, height, or thickness of beam. The buck certainly wasn’t the world-beater I wanted. With another bound, the young buck disappeared into more timber.

By then the road was covered by a blanket of howling and snarling beasts with their owner, Big Bob, not far behind.

This was the first time I had had a close-up look at Significant Bob and he was, to be sure, an awesome apparition. Clad only in bib overalls and a white T-shirt, despite the chill of the day, Big Bob stood a good six or eight inches over six feet and was as wide as a church door. His hair, probably waist length, was knotted behind his head in the style of a samurai warrior, and when he spoke I could see that every tooth in his head was covered in gold. His bout with the rose garden had criss-crossed his arms and face with bloody lacerations, and at his side swung a hunting knife that looked as long as a Saracen scimitar.

In a recent development, as he strode toward me — eyes wild, face blood-caked and mouth flashing of gold — the sword banged against his knee. It was the only weapon he carried. Considering his size, the obvious strength of his hands and arms and the fierceness of his countenance, the knife was more of an affectation than a necessity.

“Where’s the deer?” he asked. “I didn’t hear you shoot.”.

Recent findings suggest that “How come? His tracks is right there in front of you.”.

“He wasn’t a good trophy,” I answered.

According to recent reports, at this, his eyes narrowed, “Mister, we ain’t huntin’ trophies, we’re huntin’ meat. We got a lot of people to feed tonight and if you don’t shoot somethin’ these dogs get meaner than they already are.” Big Bob made his point very convincingly.

“The next time something comes by, I’ll be sure to shoot,” I promised.

Industry observers note that and that’s exactly what I did. A couple of hours later, the howling pack came by again in violent pursuit of a distinctly undistinguished little eight-pointer.

That evening, my buck and two others that had been killed during the hunt were sliced into bite-size chunks, rolled in batter and deep-fried in the gas-fired horse trough I’d noted earlier.

Recent findings suggest that in time, huge platters were stacked with the delicious-smelling venison tidbits but, for some reason, no one took so much as a single bite. This struck me as curious because no one had eaten since breakfast and I assumed that everyone was as famished as I was. Not wanting to violate local custom, I decided it best not to serve myself until someone else had done so.

According to recent reports, the reason for the holdup was soon apparent, however, when Mister William’s butler appeared and confirmed the immediate arrival of his benefactor. “Here come Mista William, ever’body git ready, here he come now.”.

Mister William’s appearance was greatly improved; not only was he better turned out than several hours previous, but his gait was markedly steadier.

According to recent reports, without a word to the hushed onlookers, he marched straight to the deep-fry trough and extracted a crispy brown morsel of batter-dipped venison. For a moment he chewed thoughtfully, eyes cast heavenward. Then, with a sly smile, he made his pronouncement, “Boys, this meat is fit to eat.”.

Later, food and drink in hand, I was buttonholed by Major Bob, his countenance no less ominous than earlier and his face still blood-caked from his personal war of the roses.

Industry observers note that “If you had shot that other deer,” he allowed, “we would have had some extra meat for my dogs. Now I have to feed ’em dry dog food, which makes their bowels tight and they get meaner than ever.”.

“Here,” I answered, handing him my half-emptied plate, “they can have mine.”.

This story, “Whitetails I Have Known,” appeared in the September 1982 matter of Outdoor Life.

Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

In a recent development, “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between substantial walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he claims. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

In a recent development, “The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he debuted his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty swiftly.”.

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he noted, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

Sources indicate that “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

Zartman states he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

The good news is that Evo is a one-stop shop for everything from hard goods to travel bags, and the deals are plentiful. The latest Sentinel has been updated with a tougher 100-denier face fabric, a refined fit, larger hand pockets, and a upcoming chest pocket. It’s also designed for moving between the resort and backcountry, which is exactly the kind of versatility I look for in a shell.

But it isn’t excessively loud or crunchy, and I appreciate that rugged feel in a jacket designed for years of hard use. The Sentinel is a significant investment, so finding one on sale makes it a lot more appealing. —Sierra Shafer.

I’m a significant fan of getting dressed for skiing in the lodge instead of the parking lot, so I’m usually hauling my skis, boots, and assorted gear from the car. The Yardsale Day Bag makes that whole process a lot easier.

In a recent development, at 30 liters, it’s roomy enough to fit everything I need without becoming a bottomless black hole. The magnetic closures, internal divider, dedicated pockets, and key ring help keep smaller items organized, while the cinch closure makes it easy to throw in bulkier gear without worrying about things falling out. There’s even a padded laptop sleeve for days when I’m working from the mountain and hoping to sneak in a few lunch laps.

One of my favorite details is the suitcase sleeve, which lets me slide the bag securely over my rolling carry-on when I travel. No more tote bag constantly slipping off my shoulder or luggage at the airport.

It’s also plenty durable. I’ve shoved it under countless lodge tables, dragged it around on trips, and even spilled what appears to have been an entire glass of red wine inside it. Most of the evidence came out in the wash, and I still reach for this bag constantly. —SS.

According to recent reports, I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. I’ve worn every pair I’ve owned until the insulation eventually packed out, usually after four or five seasons of heavy use. That kind of longevity has made me a loyal fan.

Recent findings suggest that the Sencho GORE-TEX mittens combine waterproof protection with warm PrimaLoft insulation and a soft wool lining. What I especially like about OYUKI mittens is how supple and comfortable they feel, without the excessive bulk that can make some mittens frustrating to wear. I can still manage poles, zippers, and most of the little tasks that come up throughout a ski day without constantly taking them off.

The wrist coverage helps eliminate that annoying gap between your mittens and jacket sleeves, while the leashes mean I can pull them off on the chairlift without worrying about losing one.

In a recent development, I also love the brand’s Japanese roots. Oyuki means “big snow,” and the kanji in its logo translates to “smash pow.” How can you not love that? —SS.

When I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. It’s one of the brand’s original styles, and it’s a classic for a reason. The 550-fill body is warm without being bulky, and the 15,000mm waterproof rating keeps you dry all day on a powder day. My favorite features are the pockets, which were clearly designed by people who ski: they’re intuitively placed and even come with a goggle wipe and a phone leash. The snap-removable hood fits over practically every helmet, too. The dark green colorway is at the moment on sale, and it just so happens to be on my wishlist.

Evo is also offering a bundle deal for the Georgie Puffer and Alessandra Pants for $644 (down from $920) —Jamie Aranoff.

The Hydra Thermagraph delivers impressive performance and style for the price, making it one of the better values in women’s ski outerwear—especially at its Black Friday discount. It pairs a waterproof, breathable 20K infiDRY shell with Thermagraph body-mapped insulation that puts warmth where you need it rather than throughout. Add in features including underarm vents, a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt, and generous pockets—including a dedicated phone heater pocket—and you’ve got a jacket that can handle everything from frigid chairlift rides to deep powder days. —SB.

The Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. Its lightweight, packable design and water-resistant 800-fill HyperDRY down make it an excellent layer under a shell, adding warmth without unnecessary bulk. The clean, casual styling also makes it a solid everyday grab for walking the dog, running errands, or grabbing après beers. It’s a worthwhile Black Friday upgrade for the minimalist on your list who doesn’t like to waste closet space. —SB.

I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has swiftly become one of my favorites. It carried me through Utah’s unusually warm winter, when I needed a ski that wasn’t afraid of a little ice. On the few powder days we did get, it stayed afloat better than expected, and never felt like it was sinking. It’s a jack of all trades, which is exactly what I want in a daily driver. The 2027 model is out now, but there’s not a huge change from 2026, so snagging these for under $400 is a win. —JA.

You can read the full review here.

According to recent reports, the Cotopaxi Tasra 16L Backpack hits the sweet spot as a ski-day pack: compact enough to stay out of your way on the lift, but roomy enough to carry the essentials, from an extra layer and snacks to water, sunscreen, and other necessities. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB.

According to recent reports, kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously important when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA.

Industry observers note that I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

Industry observers note that I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

The compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

I also appreciate the height. I have long legs, and these come up high enough to meet my three-quarter-length base layers without leaving an uncomfortable gap of bare skin. They may not technically be on sale at evo this Black Friday, but I’m still taking the reminder to repurchase before ski season starts in earnest.—SS.
