#149121. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Recent findings suggest that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • In a recent development, behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Recent findings suggest that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

In a recent development, behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

In a recent development, posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

It has been revealed that when he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he claims. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

Industry observers note that “The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

According to recent reports, mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

In a recent development, infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

Industry observers note that “Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Industry observers note that mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

Industry observers note that by the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees notes. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

Sources indicate that “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

In a recent development, scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

Sources indicate that as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Sources indicate that without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

Industry observers note that while sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

In a recent development, glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

According to recent reports, over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he notes. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Sources indicate that since the collapse of the glacier, a latest group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he notes. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque indicates, “but mountain sports have not.”.

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque states the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he claims.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily noted yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Sources indicate that looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

It has been revealed that there are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

The breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

The 7 Most Desperate Things I’ve Done in My Search for Ski Boots That Fit

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, seven states, two countries, three acupuncturists, and one orthopedist later, a skier with hard-to-fit feet found the bootfitter she needed. (Photo: Courtesy Abigail Barronian).

Recent findings suggest that overview: This first-person essay follows one skier’s years-long search for ski boots that fit, with bootfitters in seven states and two countries, a visit to an orthopedist, three acupuncturists, and a stranger’s garage. It’s a funny account of what hard-to-fit feet can drive a person to do, and a reminder that the right bootfitter can change everything.

Sources indicate that in my quest for ski boots that fit, I’ve seen bootfitters in at least seven states and two countries. I’ve visited Evo and REI, small independent shops, local chains, and garages-turned-ski shops. I’ve consulted boot designers, brand reps, professional athletes, and gear reviewers; tried Intuitions, ZipFits, and custom footbeds. I’ve seen one orthopedic doctor, three acupuncturists, and two physical therapists. I’ve stayed up at night thinking about boots, and developed recurring stress dreams about them.

Last season, I was beginning to consider looping in a tarot reader or astrologer. Maybe I needed a psychotherapist, or a priest. Maybe I’d have to just quit skiing. And then, finally, I found my bootfitter. But not before resorting to some questionable behavior along the way. Here are seven desperate things I did in my search for a bootfitter who could solve my ski boot complications.

Every pair of ski boots I wore from ages two through 22 were hand-me-downs from my older brothers. Then I started working in the ski industry. While skiing around Big Sky during a media event, a kind man working for Nordica looked at my feet with a frown.

“What are those?” he asked. I was sliding around in some decade-old size 26.5 monstrosities. He shook his head and invited me to swing by the Nordica headquarters in Fresh Hampshire. There, he measured my feet and sent me off with a pair of 25.5 Nordica Promachines.

Everything changed. Suddenly I was in an aggressive stance, my shins met real resistance, my power transfer improved dramatically. I got a taste of what a good boot can do, shortly before developing a wicked case of tendonitis in my ankles and shins.

In a recent development, after two seasons of excruciating, day-ending pain, I booked an appointment with an orthopedic foot and ankle specialist. I knew my boots were the culprit, and couldn’t be sure a doctor would understand the whole foot-encased-in-rigid-plastic thing. I lugged a giant bag with both my alpine and touring boots into the orthopedic practice and pulled them out for show-and-tell.

Industry observers note that the physician kindly assured me he knew what ski boots were, and that I wasn’t dealing with any serious medical complications. I’d have to take my boots back where they belonged.

The owner of Santa Fe’s one dedicated ski shop sized me down yet again, into the stiffest 24.5 he had on hand—a 110 from Fischer. I felt like I was skiing in socks and a vise-grip at the same time, and I lost feeling in my feet on the first lap. Mercifully, he let me return them.

Recent findings suggest that I’d hit the central problem: boots significant enough to be comfortable gave me tendonitis, and boots small enough to prevent it gave me bunions and nerve pain. So I took my boots to Taos Bootdoctors, where a whole team of bootfitters worked patiently to expand the forefoot. I’d ski for a day or two and come back, over and over, looking for just a few more millimeters. I brought six-packs and did my best to be charming, and the lovely staff never made me feel less important than the tourists dropping thousands of dollars on gear. Still, I couldn’t finish a day without pain.

Sources indicate that I soldiered through the season, eyeing an upcoming hut trip with dread. I could manage shorter tours, but a week of daylong missions posed some real problems. Once we were in the mountains, I knew no amount of bunion donuts and anti-inflammatories would save me. I had to instate boots-off breaks in the middle of eight-hour ski days, carefully pulling my socked feet out of jail and propping them up on a backpack in the snow while my friends took an extra lap. Sweet, stupid relief.

Finally, I heard a rumor about a man in Seattle working out of his garage who was willing to do unorthodox things to ski boots. He had a history of custom-fitting plug boots for ski racers, which seemed like a good sign. While visiting family in Washington, I brought him both pairs of boots.

Sources indicate that he looked at my feet, listened patiently, and rattled off a comprehensive plan that involved several devices I’d never seen before. Overnight, he molded both pairs into a completely upcoming shape. I never had to touch either boot again, and proceeded with great pleasure to ski 12-hour days in the backcountry and endless resort laps with happy feet. I had found him—the bootfitter I was looking for. Then, he retired.

When my touring boots started to go, I bought a replacement pair and nobody could make them fit. The experience began to take on mythic proportions. I felt like the princess with a pea beneath her many mattresses, or an ugly stepsister trying to cram her foot into a crystal slipper: all discomfort and wrong fit.

Recent findings suggest that it seemed my trusty Tecnicas were the problem. I tried on every touring boot at ski shops in three states. I ordered over a dozen pairs online, obsessively double-checking return policies and momentarily racking up a very scary credit card bill. Eventually, I came crawling back to my old Tecnicas with no blueprint, two full seasons into the search.

I hesitated to say yes to ski trips, afraid I’d have to sit out ski days because of pain or busted gear. Eventually, it happened: I took my tired old touring boots to Rogers Pass in B.C. and, on day three, broke the upper cuff clean off the bottom section of the boot. Thankfully we were just a few hundred yards from the truck. I spent the entire day sitting at the trailhead.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, my alpine boots had begun to warp. I found a replacement pair and was back at square one: home in Upcoming Mexico, with two pairs of ski boots that didn’t fit, rapidly dwindling patience, and no bootfitter.

Industry observers note that I considered that this might be the end of the road for me as a skier. Then, I learned that one of the best skiers I know had been contemplating quitting the sport because of foot pain. He’d even gone so far as to teach himself to snowboard. But then he found exactly what I’d been looking for: yet another fit-obsessed industry veteran working out of his garage.

In a recent development, I visited another home workshop in western Washington and the bootfitter listened carefully as I explained the problem. Then, he overhauled both pairs of boots, tirelessly stretching the forefoots to give my feet room to breathe. They took on a completely latest shape: generous and wide. I took both pairs out for a spin and sighed in relief.

There are a lot of great bootfitters out there. But for a freak like me, I’ve learned I need something of a mad scientist. If you’re plagued with bone spurs, high insteps, wide feet—there’s hope, I promise. With a little faith, a lot of persistence, and maybe something like divine intervention, I trust you’ll find the bootfitter you need. Let’s just hope they don’t retire.

#149114. Industry News: Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2308 w)

Industry News: Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2308 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • It has been revealed that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
  • According to recent reports, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

It has been revealed that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

According to recent reports, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

According to recent reports, for example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

In a recent development, I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

In a recent development, quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Recent findings suggest that required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only enhancement is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Recent findings suggest that better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

Sources indicate that if you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

It has been revealed that get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-newly introduced isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are key. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

Recent findings suggest that this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being remarked, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

It has been revealed that A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

Sources indicate that the crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Sources indicate that waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

Gary Colliver Was a “Substantial-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • It has been revealed that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • In a recent development, throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

It has been revealed that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

In a recent development, throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

It has been revealed that to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions remarked. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

In a recent development, colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management initiative for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

“There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial proposal was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

According to recent reports, as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular major wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

#149108. Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1539 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • Industry observers note that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

Industry observers note that “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing significant things.”.

Sources indicate that actually, major is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

It has been revealed that there’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

“I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a major challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

Recent findings suggest that she also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

In a recent development, the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

Recent findings suggest that “I just set it and left it,” she mentioned. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she stated. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

According to recent reports, “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she stated. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

Sources indicate that she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she mentioned. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

In a recent development, the temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

Industry observers note that “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she stated of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling initiative: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

Recent findings suggest that as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she noted.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

In a recent development, and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

Industry observers note that “I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case stated. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

#149105. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2355 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • Recent findings suggest that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • According to recent reports, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

Recent findings suggest that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

According to recent reports, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

According to recent reports, I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and promptly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

In a recent development, I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

In a recent development, the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

Industry observers note that as excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

Sources indicate that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

Recent findings suggest that at that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

According to recent reports, I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

It has been revealed that the climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Industry observers note that around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

According to recent reports, at 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we rapidly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

#149104. Controversial Senate Bill Would Speed Up Development on Public Lands

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1769 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fieldandstream ↗ Open Full Page

Controversial Senate Bill Would Speed Up Development on Public Lands

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with substantial implications for America’s federally managed public lands.
  • Mike Lee (R-UT), BAAJA has drawn widespread criticism from conservationists, environmentalists, and public land advocates, with groups from the Wilderness Society to the National Wildlife Federation speaking out in opposition.
  • It has been revealed that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 19, the United State Senate passed a sweeping 400-page bill with substantial implications for America’s federally managed public lands. Called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—or BAAJA for short—the bill would ease permitting restrictions for all sorts of public-land development projects, from mining and drilling to large-scale solar farms and geothermal power projects. Supporters say it would open the door for more clean-energy projects on public lands while reducing utility costs for American consumers.

Co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT), BAAJA has drawn widespread criticism from conservationists, environmentalists, and public land advocates, with groups from the Wilderness Society to the National Wildlife Federation speaking out in opposition. According to the National Council of American Indians, it has also caused serious concerns in tribal nations across the country.

It has been revealed that A large portion of the bill aims to reform or streamline the permitting process that developers must adhere to when applying for projects on federal public lands. It would do so by shrinking the scope, timelines, and legal challenges presently available under both the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Clean Water Act (CWA).

In an October blog post, the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership (TRCP) mentioned “permitting reform rules decide how a pipeline, transmission line, mine or dam gets approved, whether hunters and anglers have any say in where it goes—and what happens to elk winter range, trout streams or migration corridors in their path.”.

While TRCP has stopped short of publicly opposing the bill, they did highlight several concerns in the post. For starters, they flagged a provision in the bill—Section 1401—that “would make it much more challenging to fix problems once a project is permitted.”.

Titled “Project Certainty,” this section of the BAAJA bill would restrict federal agencies—like the Bureau of Land Management or the US Forest Service—from revoking previously issued permits during future presidential administrations. Critics say this section of the bill could lock in controversial projects—like a proposed copper-sulfide mine on the edge of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the 211-mile Ambler mining road that the Department of the Interior (DOI) is pushing for Alaska’s Brooks Range.

In a separate blog post, Backcountry Hunters & Anglers (BHA) highlighted similar concerns with the “Project Certainty” provision in the BAAJA bill. “For BHA, this raises questions about whether federal land managers would retain sufficient flexibility to respond to changing conditions and protect public resources over the long term,” the BHA post states. “For example, if a mining project near Minnesota’s Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness received federal approval, these provisions could limit a future administration’s ability to revisit that approval in response to newly identified impacts on water quality or fisheries, depending on the circumstances and applicable legal exceptions.”.

Aaron Kindle is the Director of Sporting Advocacy at the National Wildlife Federation (NWF). He tells Field & Stream that NWF opposes the BAAJA bill in its current form because it raises too many questions, is moving too fast without adequate public awareness, and it undermines key public-land safeguards.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a hugely consequential bill happening during a lame-duck session with very little public understanding,” Kindle says. “[NWF] is pro-permitting reform. But when we do the analysis on this, and we talk to other conservation friends and partners, it’s just too fraught.”.

Industry observers note that kindle notes NWF shares both BHA’s and TRCP’s concerns around the bill’s project certainty guarantees for developers. “It shortens review timelines, it narrows what triggers a review, and it kind of locks it in once it’s done,” he says. “We’ve always wanted to be able to do adaptive management on anything that’s done. Anytime you narrow environmental review parameters like this, or make permits too concrete, that’s concerning for a broad swath of our most cherished public lands and waters.”.

It has been revealed that kindle notes NWF is also worried that the bill could expedite data center construction on public lands. Up until now, no data center has been permitted on any federal public lands, though the DOI did attempt to approve one on BLM lands in Nevada back in August, before a federal appeals court revoked the permit.

“What we’ve understood so far is that [BAAJA] shields [data center developers] from future regulations and makes it hard, or maybe even impossible, to revoke the permits once they’ve been awarded,” he adds. “What if we learn at some future point that these things are incredibly harmful to water, air, wildlife, the grid, who knows—and then they’re just locked in place, and there’s nothing we can do about it?”.

The Wilderness Society has been one of the most vocal opponents of the BAAJA bill since it first started making headlines in early November. Wilderness Society President, Tracy Stone-Manning, who ran the BLM during the Biden Administration, calls the bill alarming.

Recent findings suggest that “Some of the places that hang in the balance are the Boundary Waters in northern Minnesota and the Brooks Range of Alaska, because of the proposed Ambler Road and Arctic Mine, the entire Alaskan Arctic really, and all of that caribou habitat,” Stone-Manning tells F&S. “You’ve also got places in the Lower 48, like the Roan Plateau in Colorado with its amazing mule deer and elk herds, which sportsmen and women fought so hard to protect, and the headwaters of Montana’s Bitterroot River, where they want to build a rare-earth mine up on Sheep Creek. Whatever the Trump Administration decides to do in these places in the next two years, that gets locked in if this bill passes. We won’t be able to undo it.”.

The Wilderness Society supports expanded permitting for renewable energy projects on public lands, which have declined steeply during the first two years of the Trump Administration. But for Stone-Manning, the risks of the BAAJA bill far outweigh the rewards.

Recent findings suggest that “The bottom line is, this bill takes away environmental safeguards for habitat and gives developers certainty,” she says. “Those two things coupled together spell disaster for our country’s conservation heritage and for our public-land hunting and fishing traditions.”.

In a recent development, many conservationists who opposes BAAJA are confused by Sen. Martin Heinrich’s staunch support for the bill. Heinrich has been one of the Senate’s most stalwart defenders of public lands for years. He has helped secure Wilderness Area and National Monument status for thousands of acres of public lands in his home state of New Mexico, for example. More recently, he was a vocal and outspoken opponent of an attempt to sell off more than 3.4 million acres of Western public lands in the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”.

Recent findings suggest that today, he’s defending BAAJA in the halls of Congress and in the op-ed pages of major news outlets like the New York Times and the Economist. In a recent interview with Field & Stream, Heinrich cited an urgent need to slow climate change as his primary motivator for helping craft and co-sponsoring the legislation.

“This will allow us to put green energy on the grid at a scale where we might be able to mitigate the worst future outcomes of climate change,” Heinrich claims. “I’ve realized that I’m watching the world change at such a pace, that if we don’t get to work on this, I don’t know what kind of world my grandkids are going to inherit. The places that I fish in New Mexico, for example, are changing. We don’t have a lot of water. If these places go away, and we don’t have snowpack, we’re done. It’s game over.”.

Industry observers note that heinrich states the bill address climate change by putting public land renewable projects—like wind, solar, and geothermal—on equal footing with oil, gas, and mining. “We want to bring renewables into the same regulatory permitting regime that the fossil fuel projects already have,” he says. “Right now, oil and gas in particular, and natural gas pipelines, have a sort of privileged position.”.

Industry observers note that heinrich disputes claims from his critics that the bill weakens key public-land safeguards like NEPA and the Clean Water Act. And he indicates it won’t expedite or lock-in mining permits in the Boundary Waters.

In a recent development, “We don’t change or lower standards in this bill; we streamline the process,” he says. “If you’re a mine developer, you still have to get your Clean Water Act permit, and it doesn’t change the standard for that. When you look at the Boundary Waters, what I don’t see is that project being able to clear is a state Clean Water Act permit, because I just don’t think it will be possible to do mining with open-air tailings at that site—having seen it with my own eyes—without the acid generated making it into the water next door.”.

According to recent reports, heinrich also disagrees with BAAJA opponents who say the bill will open the door for data center development on public lands. “I don’t think that data centers belong on public lands, and I think any effort to build them on public lands is probably a legal stretch of existing authorizations and presidential authorities,” he adds. “This bill just makes data centers pay their fair freight for attaching to the grid, instead of passing that cost on to everyday consumers in the form higher electricity rates.”.

The Trump Administration’s current policy around data centers is murky at best. But recent reporting from the Washington Sun revealed that the BLM was reviewing at least 12 data center proposals spread across 17,600 acres of public land in six western states. In its recent strategic plan, DOI, which manages close to 500 million acres of public land, listed data center development as a top priority, alongside the potential transfer or sale of federal public lands to states and local governments.

According to recent reports, sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) tried to attach an amendment to the bill that would have banned the construction of data centers on public lands altogether when the Senate was debating BAAJA earlier this month. That effort ultimately failed and Wyden voted against the bill, though it still passed the full Senate on 63-33 vote.

In a recent development, president Trump endorsed the bill in a recent Truth Social post and remarked he’ll sign it if it comes across his desk, calling it a big win for energy independence and dominance. Now its awaiting a vote in the US House of Representatives. House members could vote as early as next week, when they return from Thanksgiving recess.
