Smartwool Active Fleece Wind Headband.

Black Diamond Astro 300-R Headlamp.

Sources indicate that there’s nothing more delightful than rummaging around in an oversized sock to find a piece of backpacking gear you never knew you needed. Even if your giftee isn’t overwhelmed with joy (we’re sure they will be), these micro-gifts won’t set you back like an expensive, ill-fitting sleeping bag might. From energy chews to our current favorite pocket knife, here are ten backpacker-tested stocking stuffers, all small enough to fit into a hipbelt pocket.

Hydration and electrolytes are a stacked category, but we love that Tailwind uses easy-to-drink, naturally-flavored mixes instead of unpronounceable ingredients. The 25-serving bulk bag is a good economical choice, but if single-serving packets are more convenient, you can opt for a variety pack instead. For super sweaty hikers, Saltt drink mixes add a dose of sodium to the blend without making it taste like seawater.

Hiking hard in the heat can be a recipe for an upset stomach, but hikers still have to eat enough to power their miles. Skratch’s energy chews are some of the easiest to get down thanks to the varied texture of the sour sugar coating and punchy flavors. Choose between caffeinated and non-caffeinated varieties, all with easy-to-digest carbs for a quick boost of energy that doesn’t entail gnawing on a dense protein bar.

Sources indicate that A headband might not seem like a thrilling gift, but no one is ever sad they threw it into their pack. Smartwool’s version is warm and wicking, blocking brisk winds around the forehead with a windproof panel and extra width around the ears for coverage. This is the perfect accessory for chilly-but-not-frigid hikes where a beanie is overkill, but the wind is turning your forehead into an ice cube.

Recent findings suggest that leatherman might be best known for its ranch-ready multitools, but it also has a lovely line of reliable, lightweight pocket knives. The Skeletool KB weighs just over one ounce, has a built-in bottle opener, and a tensioned belt clip for securing to a pocket or an interior flap on your pack. We’ve carried this for weeks at a time without seeing any dulling or corrosion. If you want to go massive, you can also spring for a high-end Benchmade Bugout Knife, which weighs 1.85 ounces and has a range of customization options.

Remember being a kid and groaning when you got socks for Christmas? Those days are long gone—we don’t know any hiker who isn’t thrilled to unwrap a fresh pair of wool socks. These trail-ready socks have a moderate amount of cushioning and structure for support without feeling compressive. Made with 75-percent merino, they also have excellent odor-resistance and softness while still holding their shape.

In a recent development, hydraPak has made impressive strides in its line of ultralight, packable filters in the past few years. This filter-and-bottle combination uses their flagship soft flask with one of our favorite hollow-fiber filters. The flow rate stays strong and fast for longer than other similar styles, and the tough, seam-welded TPU bottle can withstand a whole lot of squeezing. The wide mouth makes it easy to fill, and hikers can either squeeze it into a larger bottle for drinking water or drink directly from the filter.

Black Diamond nailed it with this headlamp. The Astro 300 offers an excellent combination of low weight (just 2.65 ounces), night-hiker-approved 300-lumen output, and a conveniently integrated rechargeable battery, all at a reasonable price. It’s highly waterproof and durable for long, rugged outings, and the single button is easy to press while wearing gloves. The only downside is that it doesn’t include a red light. If that’s an problem, Nitecore’s UT27 MCT Pro 800 is more expensive, but weighs the same and comes with a red light option.

According to recent reports, though it gets less press than rolled ankles and bad knees, skin chafing is the sneaky destroyer of many good days on the trail. Keep your hiker’s inner thighs safe with a stick of Squirrel’s Nut Butter, which has a trimmed-down formula limited to natural ingredients like coconut oil, cocoa butter, and Vitamin E oil. It glides on smoothly, and each application lasts several hours. Fast-packers and people in more humid environments might also appreciate Run Slick, which has a roll-on formula that is among the most sweat-resistant we’ve ever tested.

According to recent reports, even the most weight-conscious backpacker will spare a few grams in the food bag for instant coffee. Alpine Start dissolves in a flash in hot water, and can even be shaken up without gritty residue in colder water for iced coffee vibes. The brand uses single-origin beans from farms in Colombia, and each packet is perfect for 8-10 ounces of water.

According to recent reports, wired headphones might be a technological relic, but for backpackers, the trend never died. We love the convenience of having one less thing to charge on the trail, and this pair from Skullcandy has excellent sound quality for a reasonable price. They’re also durable: The cords on our pair have survived over a month of daily use on-trail without separating. If you’re looking to splurge, Bose recently updated its flagship wired earbuds, and the bump in price gets you better noise-canceling and a clear in-line microphone for ordering pizza to the trailhead.

#149059. The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Latest Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Vital Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1693 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting Latest Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Vital Than Ever.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc.
  • The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees.
  • Sources indicate that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A view of the of the Alps on Tour du Mont Blanc. (Photo: Getty).

The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Sources indicate that moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

Recent findings suggest that chamonix and the six other French towns along the TMB route, from Vallorcine to Bourg-Saint-Maurice and Beaufort, have drafted a charter to manage crowds, with local officials aiming to put it in place by spring 2027, ahead of next year’s trekking season. The newly introduced rules, aiming to curb overtourism and help slow environmental damage, are awaiting final signature. The key proposals include reservations for every night on the trail; a ban on wild camping, with paid, bookable bivouac areas replacing the informal spots; and new limits on luggage transfers. Guided groups would be capped at twelve and led by guides trained in rescue and licensed in all three countries.

The charter is voluntary, covers only France for now, and still depends on local ordinances for enforcement. But the message is clear: the era of showing up and figuring it out on the TMB is ending. Chamonix’s mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, who is similarly introducing quotas at nearby Lac Blanc, an alpine lake also suffering from its popularity, puts it this way: “To reserve is to preserve.”.

Adding to the growing traffic on the trail are the effects of climate change on the Alps. Rising summer temperatures are accelerating permafrost thaw and glacier retreat, contributing to record rockfall activity in the Mont Blanc massif. While this mostly impacts the summit climbing routes, hot summers also change trail and water conditions for hikers on the Tour du Mont Blanc.

“As for the environmental impacts, trail erosion is of course the most obvious one, but we must also take into account wild bivouacking, which has multiplied, with impacts on the flora as well as the disturbance of wildlife,” notes Daniel Rodrigues, general director of the Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix, the oldest mountain guide organization in the world.

“The reservation system is fair. Everyone can book their places, and tour operators can do the same. So the same rules apply to everyone, including amateur mountain people, and that matters to us: the mountains are a space of freedom,” says Rodrigues. “That said, this space must be protected, in terms of biodiversity and environmental impacts, but also economically.”.

The charter puts licensed mountain professionals at the center of safety on the trail. According to Rodrigues, that means operators will no longer be able to sell self-guided packages (just bookings and transfers) and will have to include a guide certified in all three countries.

Sources indicate that “This is a major step forward, because the guide ensures that everyone stays safe and that everything goes smoothly. It also creates work for local people and delivers a genuine positive impact on the inhabitants of this mountain range,” adds Rodrigues.

I hiked the Tour du Mont Blanc in August with Live Breathe Hike, and I came home convinced that, especially under the potential latest rules, having a local guide is no longer a luxury. It’s the smartest way to hike this trail.

The TMB isn’t one trail; rather, there are a lot of different paths and detours.”There’s a classic route, but there’s a lot of different variants,” says Allison Fleece, cofounder of WHOA Travel, a women’s adventure-travel firm that runs guided trips, including on the Tour du Mont Blanc. Some variants are higher and more exposed; others go along lower valleys. On our third day, instead of following the crowds, Day led us off the Col du Bonhomme on a variant toward Lac de Roselend, where we barely saw another hiker for miles. “You feel like you have the place to yourself,” says Live Breathe Hike founder Tanya Perret, who started the Chamonix-based trekking company in 2016 and says she has guided the TMB more than 75 times.

Recent findings suggest that under the proposed rules, every night would have to be booked in advance, across three countries with different systems. Guides already do that work, and finding gems to stay at like Le Chalet de Roselend takes deep knowledge of the area. With only ten rooms, the chalet, whose balconies overlook the Lac de Roselend, was a godsend after one of our longest days of trekking. Years ago, Perret drove there to book it in person, because the elderly owner at the time only took reservations face to face. The young couple who now runs it cooks traditional dishes with local produce.

Industry observers note that the charter asks operators to buy local and partner with local producers. Good guides already do. “Many of the places that we stay are generational families, and I’ve known those families for 30 years,” indicates Perret. On our trip, that meant a stop at a family cheese farm as well as the small lakeside chalet. “That’s the micro-economy,” adds Perret.

Nearly every day on my trek, Day chose a variant. Perret says the choice comes down to two factors: where accommodation is available and which trail will give the group the best experience that day.

The variants usually turned out to be my favorite stretches. Self-guided trekkers can research the variants, but a guide knows which one fits the day. “By giving your guides a little bit of autonomy, it means they can just tweak things here and there, which makes for a unique journey,” says Perret.

Industry observers note that “The weather patterns change a lot in the mountains and they change really fast,” adds Fleece, who partners with Compagnie des Guides de Chamonix on their guided TMB trips. “Guides have years and years, most of the time decades, of experience.” A guide, she notes, can help you avoid dicey situations, “but also, if you get yourself into a dicey situation, having a guide is like a safety measure to get you promptly and swiftly out of it.”.

Sources indicate that day has been trekking Tour Du Mont Blanc since 1992 and knows the ever-changing mountain conditions demand quick judgment. On a recent trip up Mont Blanc’s Italian route, he and his climbing partner turned back in poor snow. “We binned the whole trip,” he states. Two friends kept going, and on a ridge with snow cornices on both sides, one side broke away. “Either side could have gone,” he says.

Multi-day treks around the world are my favorite way to travel. With WHOA, I’ve summited Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, Europe’s tallest peak (not Mont Blanc, as many assume). I’ve taken guided trips on the Trans Bhutan Trail and Japan’s Shikoku pilgrimage, which were not nearly as challenging but would have been far less rich experiences without learning the culture from our local guides. I’ve trekked the full O Trek in Patagonia without a guide, but with friends and the help of the tech giant Chile Nativo for booking refuges. Half of the O circuit, the W Trek, I hiked alone. So I know the benefits of taking guided multi-day treks and hiking alone at your own pace, stopping when you want.

I can understand why travelers would want to do the TMB without a guide; many hikers do so without any issue. You can go at your own speed and take a long break for an afternoon coffee at a refuge with an open table facing the sun. A guided trip costs more. Middle options have been growing, including self-guided packages that handle the bookings for you, but even those require your due diligence and research, and could be affected by these new rules for 2027.

One day on the trek, we stopped for lunch at a refuge and ran into a woman with a bandaged hand. She and her friend were on a self-guided trip whose itinerary, she told us, had started them on their first day hiking one of the route’s most exposed stretches—the ladders below Tête aux Vents—where she got injured. On the standard counterclockwise route, that section usually comes at the very end. Day told us that those ladders can easily be bypassed in busy seasons or wet weather.

It has been revealed that if you want to escape the crowds on the Tour du Mont Blanc, guides know the variants that lead to the quietest parts of the trail. Except for a few days, on certain passes, we managed to find stretches where it was just us, as far as I  could see. On our fourth day, we crossed the Col de la Seigne into Italy, past a block of granite barely knee-high: the real border marker, not the substantial monument nearby. I’d have walked right past it. My guide didn’t let me.

After a year of hiking, camping, running, and climbing, there’s a good chance everyone on your list is dealing with an adventure-related ailment: a stiff back, a beat-up foot, a gnarly sunburn, a killer headache.

Industry observers note that gone are the days of slathering greasy lotion on your arms and back. With UPF 50+, REI Co-op’s classic shade hoodie prevents sun damage on long backcountry days and summertime runs. Even with the head-to-hips coverage, the sweat-wicking polyester-spandex blend will keep you dry. Thumbholes and a hood drawstring ensure the stretchy hoodie stays put as you jog, climb, or cycle. Bonus: The women’s style has a vent on the back of the hood that doubles as a ponytail outlet.

Pound the pavement, then treat your tender feet to plush recovery slides. OOFOS’ proprietary foam is designed to absorb 37 percent more shock than similar shoes on the market, and the footbed cradles your heel to further minimize impact. When foul smells and grime inevitably build up, toss the spongy slides in the washing machine and air-dry.

One of our top-rated hot yoga mats, the Liforme mat has a grippy surface that’s unrivaled. “When I practice on this mat in a heated room, I don’t need a towel and rarely need to wipe my hands to make sure I don’t slip,” one of our testers reported. Extra credit for the alignment lines and larger-than-conventional dimensions.

The silence created with noise-canceling headphones can feel unsettling. These analog silicone ear plugs reduce noise by 14 decibels—that’s the volume difference between running a vacuum and a dishwasher—so you still have the comfort of background noise as you work from a coffee shop or camp solo. The included carry case keeps the ear tips from becoming a home for the dust bunnies at the bottom of your tote bag.

Upgrade your mobility routine with a body roller built to minimize spine discomfort. The high-density foam roller’s center groove allows your spine to relax while you perform thoracic extensions or massage the lats, traps, and rhomboids. After hitting the upper body, use the channel to target the IT band and Achilles tendon. Expect a particularly grippy surface thanks to the embossed diamond texture.

It has been revealed that formulated with skin-care ingredients like hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and aloe vera, this transparent stick sunscreen glides onto skin. Even tough-to-reach spots—like the sides of the nostrils and hair part—effortlessly get broad-spectrum SPF 45 protection thanks to the stick’s “teardrop” shape. Stash it in a fanny pack, hipbelt pocket, or glove compartment, and you’ll never have an excuse to not reapply.

In a recent development, reset your sleep routine with an alarm clock that doesn’t come furnished with TikTok. Power down at bedtime with Hatch’s dimmable reading lamp and calming background sounds like rain falling, a fan running, or wind blowing. Then, wake up to a “sunrise” and the gentle sounds of birds chirping, à la Snow White, or a good-morning call straight from Love Island.

Traverse open ridgelines, kayak down rivers, and train for marathons on bright pavement while keeping your peepers safe. The Tera’s polarized lenses reduce glare (goodbye, headaches) and UV400 lenses block 100 percent of UVA and UVB rays. Plus, the removable magnetic shields wrap around the sides of the recycled frames, blocking rays, dust, and snow from reaching your eyes.

Staying hydrated is always important. This Stanley tumbler makes doing so both easy and stylish, with its bold, Jeep-branded design and insulated stainless-steel construction that keeps liquids cold (or warm, if preferred) for hours on end.

The 40-ounce mug is designed with an extra-large handle and a straw that make sipping simple on the move, while the tapered bottom fits into most cupholders. It’s also dishwasher safe, so the only real question to answer is what snacks you’ll be pairing its contents with.

Ideal for the designated mom of the friend group, this whimsical mini first-aid kit packs the essentials needed for sudden cuts and scrapes: 18 flexible fabric bandages in two sizes, three antibiotic ointment packets, and three hand sanitizer packets. When empty, repurpose the pastel “tie-dyed” metal container for your patches, stickers, or tiny toiletries.

Stop wasting money on overpriced teeny toothpaste tubes. These two refillable containers allow you to bring up to a three-week supply of your paste of choice—prescription, Sensodyne, you name it—in your carry-on. Reviewers say they’re perfect for moisturizers and Vaseline, too.

In a recent development, erase the lingering pain linked to your desk job or overpacked weekender. The extra-firm tip digs deep into cranky knots, and the two massage balls allow you to simultaneously work the muscles running along both sides of your spine. Thanks to the cane-shaped design, you’re able to hit every hard-to-reach spot on your backside without needing a masseuse.

Recent findings suggest that stave off caffeine-withdrawal headaches while car camping or vacationing in an ill-equipped Airbnb. Combining the powers of pour-over, immersion, and air-pressure brewing methods, this travel coffee maker creates a smooth, rich, and full-bodied cup in just a few minutes. The entire system fits into its travel mug, making it carry-on-friendly to boot. Just remember to BYOB (bring your own beans).

Combine a pair of booties with a sleeping bag, and the result is these mules from The North Face. The slippers boast a water-repellent upper stuffed with a synthetic down-like material, similar to your winter puffer. Fleece lining the interior keeps your toes cozy, and the rubber outsole makes the mules suitable for both taking out the trash and enjoying après-ski.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge).

“How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”.

That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

Sources indicate that fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

In a recent development, I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

Fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

In a recent development, I was 52, the age when menopause, graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something big to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from the beach, I bought a hooded, five-millimeter wetsuit and booties, and started surfing several mornings a week, collecting phone numbers of women I met in the lineup and parking lot.

After decades of giving everything I had to everyone around me—work colleagues, kids, husband, dogs, parents, sisters—surfing was just for me.

Soon I had built a community of women surfers aged 25 to 75 to join me for dawn patrol sessions at our break north of San Francisco and surf trips to Mexico, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, San Diego, and Santa Cruz.

Sources indicate that surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

Seeking guidance on how to surf through surgery recovery and treatment, I posted a message on the Facebook “Women Who Surf” group of 39,000: “I just got diagnosed with breast cancer and am looking for other women surfers who surfed through chemo, and surfed after a double mastectomy.”.

According to recent reports, A hundred women weighed in with personal experience of cancer and surfing. Most hadn’t surfed during surgery recovery or chemotherapy due to doctors’ orders, infection risk, weak immune systems, limited mobility, fatigue, and weakness.

Sources indicate that but one woman told me to go for it: Melanie Ezell, a 42-year-old massive wave surfer, based in Oahu, who surfed through ovarian cancer. She became my role model, inspiring me to paddle out as soon as I could.

That long-awaited day came after being grounded on land for seven weeks following my double mastectomy. It was three days after my first chemotherapy infusion when my plastic surgeon declared my chest incisions adequately healed. I drove immediately to the beach, paddled out, and felt triumphant when I caught my first wave of the session.

And I kept paddling out through the remaining 11 rounds of chemotherapy.

On days when the swell was big and I was weak with fatigue, I’d claw through the impact zone after riding a wave, leaving my arms drained of power and lungs gasping for air. Once safely outside breaking waves, I’d rest on my board and let sets roll past until my breathing slowed. Still, being in the ocean felt like an antidote to the toxic drugs coursing through my veins. I loved watching the birds and seals, scanning the horizon for incoming sets, paddling into a rising wave, feeling its energy connect with my board.

Industry observers note that sometimes those sessions lasted only an hour because of my reduced stamina. But they always left me feeling stoked and alive, adjectives easily lost when you spend Tuesday afternoons hooked up to an IV bag pumping the sledgehammer drug Taxol into a port in your chest.

After my last chemotherapy session, I started ten rounds of targeted immunotherapy infusions (which I just concluded this month) and began posting GoPro videos on Instagram and Facebook of me surfing bald to inspire other women. I wanted them to see what it looks like when breast cancer takes your breasts and hair, but not your identity.

Women from around the world reached out to share their own stories: Ellen McLaughlin, a 54-year-old massage therapist and mom surfing through rectal cancer in the chilly waters at the Oregon-California border; 32-year-old Lottie Bakewell from Cornwall, England, surfing through breast cancer and the demands of caring for her one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter; Belen Kimble, a 48-year-old former professional longboarder, World Surf League commentator, surf performance coach, and single mom in Fresh South Wales, Australia, surfing through breast cancer; and Caroline Wilhelm, a 55-year-old surfer and competitor from Los Angeles who took my cue to keep surfing through her breast cancer.

Backed by growing research showing that physical activity during cancer treatment offsets chemotherapy side effects and improves recovery and resilience, my little cohort of surfing cancer patients proves the ocean is not just a sanctuary, but an active prescription for healing.

Industry observers note that but you don’t have to be a surfer to reap the benefits of physical activity during cancer. A new study of 45,530 women published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute in September 2026 confirmed what my surf sisters and I already knew: regular exercise gives women going through breast cancer the strength to bounce back more fully and reclaim our lives after treatment. The study followed women for 15 years with data from the Women’s Health Initiative and found that keeping up physical activity and healthy habits prior to a cancer diagnosis acts as a powerful buffer against the physical toll of cancer treatments.

The trick is to start with small amounts of exercise and work with your care team on a game strategy to get active.

“Even if you are not an exerciser, you can still start an exercise regimen during chemotherapy,” said my oncologist Eva Thomas, MD, from Kaiser Permanente Oakland in California, who encouraged and cheered on my surfing during chemotherapy. “It sounds counter-intuitive, but women tell me that when they push themselves to exercise, they feel better. Mood is better, sleep is better, energy is increased, and body aches are reduced.”.

According to recent reports, in 2022, the American Society of Clinical Oncology released the first-ever exercise guidelines based on more than 100 clinical trials examining the link between exercise and cancer treatment. For anyone going through cancer who wants to get active, the American College of Sports Medicine created a step-by-step guide in 2024 with research benefits and resources. It outlines a path to get started.

My own path began years before cancer, as a young woman fixated on surfing, who waited decades to act upon her dream.

Recent findings suggest that looking back, I see that my surfing community—and the strength and identity it gave me—helped me to charge forward through the scariest chapter of my life. The takeaway lesson is useful for all women and men facing challenges: Don’t delay trying something newly introduced and scary. It may end up transforming, and saving, you.

Danielle Cass lives with her husband in Northern California, where they raised their 26-year-old son, 23-year-old daughter, and dogs. When she’s not surfing with friends, she leads Responsible AI enablement at Microsoft. A two-minute short film about her midlife entry into surfing Learning to Surf at 52 screened at the 2022 San Diego Surf Festival. Follow her surfing through cancer adventures on Instagram @danielle.cass and Substack Danielle Rides the Cancer Wave.

#149055. The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (595 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

The Terminus of the CDT is Now Behind a Border Wall. Here’s What Hikers Can Expect

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year.
  • Sources indicate that now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls currently under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA).
  • Sources indicate that in November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail has changed a lot in the last year. The granite obelisk once stood in the open Chihuahuan Desert, in a remote area visited by few except hikers either starting or ending their journeys. The dirt road approaching it, Commodore Road, was unmaintained and required high-clearance vehicles, limiting access and traffic.

Sources indicate that now, though, the monument stands between two imposing 30-foot border walls currently under construction, in a National Defense Area (NDA). Government contractors graded and widened the road from 8 feet to 24 feet to accommodate construction vehicles. For now, hikers can still enter the NDA with permission and touch the monument—whether they’re starting northbound or ending their CDT hike. However, security guards will eventually usher them away, out of the construction zone.

Sources indicate that in November, Teresa Martinez, the executive director of the CDT Coalition (CDTC), and Audra Labert, the CDTC director of communications, traveled to the southern terminus. Neither had been there since construction began in early 2026.

“We wanted to see on the ground what was actually happening and what people were experiencing,” Martinez told Backpacker. She described the scene as “surreal.”.

Industry observers note that arriving at the terminus monument, Martinez and Labert watched as two hikers approached in the distance. The two women, trail names Geisha Girl and Fearless, marched toward them, border walls standing on both sides. In an emotional moment, the teary-eyed hikers walked right up to the monument.

Industry observers note that “I think if they hadn’t been able to put their hands on the physical monument, even though it was between the two barriers, it would have been devastating,” Martinez said. “The importance of having access to that now while it’s under construction is so fundamental.”.

Recent findings suggest that while these changes are striking to someone like Martinez, who has visited this terminus hundreds of times during her work with the non-profit trail organization, she claims she sees a silver lining. The construction traffic is annoying, loud, disruptive, and changes the experience of finishing or starting your CDT hike in a quiet corner of the desert. But the improvements to Commodore Road greatly increase access to the trail’s southern terminus.

It has been revealed that “Building a road invites more people, which means more people can get there, which is a beautiful thing. They can drive their loved ones to the trail and pick them up from the trail much easier than it ever has been,” she mentioned. But at the same time, the improvements make it feel less remote, and could make it significantly busier. “So it’s bittersweet,” she said.

Sometime “in the near future,” Martinez noted the terminus monument will be moved out of the NDA. Then, the CDTC will create a latest one with accurate longitude and latitude markers. She sees that as an opportunity to rethink how the monument will be dedicated and to include indigenous voices that weren’t involved when the original monument was dedicated in 1974.

Asked what hikers should expect when approaching the southern terminus of the CDT, Martinez paused thoughtfully.

Industry observers note that “I think they should be prepared for an amazing experience in one of the most beautiful places on the planet,” she noted. “But you’re going to see this infrastructure now that didn’t exist before. And I would ask people to lean into the good stuff and then also use that moment as an opportunity to reflect on how the experience is making them feel.”.

After a year of hiking, camping, running, and climbing, there’s a good chance everyone on your list is dealing with an adventure-related ailment: a stiff back, a beat-up foot, a gnarly sunburn, a killer headache.

This season, help take the edge off by treating them to a practical-but-appreciated health and wellness gift. These 13 goodies will relieve body aches, sleep troubles, and sun-related annoyances—or at least protect your loved ones from suffering the same fate in 2027.

Gone are the days of slathering greasy lotion on your arms and back. With UPF 50+, REI Co-op’s classic shade hoodie prevents sun damage on long backcountry days and summertime runs. Even with the head-to-hips coverage, the sweat-wicking polyester-spandex blend will keep you dry. Thumbholes and a hood drawstring ensure the stretchy hoodie stays put as you jog, climb, or cycle. Bonus: The women’s style has a vent on the back of the hood that doubles as a ponytail outlet.

Pound the pavement, then treat your tender feet to plush recovery slides. OOFOS’ proprietary foam is designed to absorb 37 percent more shock than similar shoes on the market, and the footbed cradles your heel to further minimize impact. When foul smells and grime inevitably build up, toss the spongy slides in the washing machine and air-dry.

One of our top-rated hot yoga mats, the Liforme mat has a grippy surface that’s unrivaled. “When I practice on this mat in a heated room, I don’t need a towel and rarely need to wipe my hands to make sure I don’t slip,” one of our testers reported. Extra credit for the alignment lines and larger-than-conventional dimensions.

The silence created with noise-canceling headphones can feel unsettling. These analog silicone ear plugs reduce noise by 14 decibels—that’s the volume difference between running a vacuum and a dishwasher—so you still have the comfort of background noise as you work from a coffee shop or camp solo. The included carry case keeps the ear tips from becoming a home for the dust bunnies at the bottom of your tote bag.

Upgrade your mobility routine with a body roller built to minimize spine discomfort. The high-density foam roller’s center groove allows your spine to relax while you perform thoracic extensions or massage the lats, traps, and rhomboids. After hitting the upper body, use the channel to target the IT band and Achilles tendon. Expect a particularly grippy surface thanks to the embossed diamond texture.

Formulated with skin-care ingredients like hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and aloe vera, this transparent stick sunscreen glides onto skin. Even tough-to-reach spots—like the sides of the nostrils and hair part—effortlessly get broad-spectrum SPF 45 protection thanks to the stick’s “teardrop” shape. Stash it in a fanny pack, hipbelt pocket, or glove compartment, and you’ll never have an excuse to not reapply.

Reset your sleep routine with an alarm clock that doesn’t come furnished with TikTok. Power down at bedtime with Hatch’s dimmable reading lamp and calming background sounds like rain falling, a fan running, or wind blowing. Then, wake up to a “sunrise” and the gentle sounds of birds chirping, à la Snow White, or a good-morning call straight from Love Island.

Traverse open ridgelines, kayak down rivers, and train for marathons on bright pavement while keeping your peepers safe. Plus, the removable magnetic shields wrap around the sides of the recycled frames, blocking rays, dust, and snow from reaching your eyes.

It has been revealed that the 40-ounce mug is designed with an extra-large handle and a straw that make sipping simple on the move, while the tapered bottom fits into most cupholders. It’s also dishwasher safe, so the only real question to answer is what snacks you’ll be pairing its contents with.

Ideal for the designated mom of the friend group, this whimsical mini first-aid kit packs the essentials needed for sudden cuts and scrapes: 18 flexible fabric bandages in two sizes, three antibiotic ointment packets, and three hand sanitizer packets. When empty, repurpose the pastel “tie-dyed” metal container for your patches, stickers, or tiny toiletries.

Erase the lingering pain linked to your desk job or overpacked weekender. Recent findings suggest that combine a pair of booties with a sleeping bag, and the result is these mules from The North Face. Fleece lining the interior keeps your toes cozy, and the rubber outsole makes the mules suitable for both taking out the trash and enjoying après-ski.

#149052. The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1364 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

The 9 Best Hiking Towns to Spend Your Holidays In

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).
  • But not everyone can access hiking right out their front door.
  • With that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Photos from Terry's photostream via Flickr Creative Commons).

But not everyone can access hiking right out their front door. So why not turn your holiday break into a hiking vacation? You’ll not only get to make special festive memories outside, but you can choose the geography and even the climate.

With that in mind, we’ve put together a list of the best places for hikers to holiday. Want to spend your time traipsing through deserts, among cacti and palm trees? We’ve got you covered. Looking for a more traditional experience, with snowy trails and evergreen forests? No problem. And, of course, if you like long walks on the beach and among tropical rainforests, we’ve got just the places for you.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild weather, southwestern culture, diverse landscapes, and amazing food December temps: 40-65℉ What to expect: Both desert and mountain landscapes with rocky, sandy terrain, and no snow.

Industry observers note that for those hikers who’d rather decorate a saguaro cactus than a lodgepole pine, Tucson, Arizona is calling your name. The wildernesses around town are packed with desert flora and fauna, and crisscrossed with tons of hiking trails. This can be a tough place to explore during late spring, summer, and even into fall because it gets so scorching hot. However, in the winter, the weather is perfect for hiking, making this a prime place to spend the holidays. Beyond the trails, the food is world-renowned—Tucson has been a UNESCO City of Gastronomy for over a decade.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Fair weather, proximity to Gila National Forest and Cliff Dwellings Monument, colorful western history, and a great art scene December temps: 21-55℉ What to expect: Colder, high desert climate, with very clear weather, and tons of trails exploring the Pinos Altos and Mogollon Mountains.

Situated on the outskirts of the Gila National Forest, Silver City is a gateway to desert hiking adventures. The Continental Divide Trail passes nearby; City of Rocks State Park is just 30 miles east of town, and the famous Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument is just 44 miles north. The monument area gets over 200 cloudless nights a year, making it a prime destination for winter stargazers. If you want a warm soak after your hikes, Faywood Hot Springs and Gila Hot Springs are both close to town.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, direct access to Zion National Park, regional access to Bryce Canyon or Grand Canyon, and a lively restaurant and art scene December temps: 30-55℉ What to expect:  A striking red sandstone desert landscape and trails both in the park and outside of it.

It has been revealed that winter is Zion National Park’s slow season, and yet it’s just as beautiful as it is any other time of year. Springdale sits just outside the park’s eastern entrance and is a prime location for a hiking holiday basecamp. Not only will you have direct access to the national park and all of its trails, but there are also worthy routes around town that don’t require an entrance fee. And if you aren’t afraid of a day trip, Bryce Canyon is 86 miles away.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mild temperatures, access to Lake Mead, fun holiday atmosphere, and a historic downtown December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Wide Mojave desert terrain with rolling hills and rocky mountains, canyons, panoramic lake views, and old mining and railroad infrastructure.

The deserts of southern Nevada have a lot to offer beyond the flashing lights, casinos, and nightlife of Las Vegas. About an hour southeast of Sin City, Boulder City is a much quieter historic town that offers access to some amazing trails and outdoor recreation areas. It’s just a short drive from Boulder City to Lake Mead Recreation Area, where there are a lot of trails, walkways, and observation points. Some hikes close to town are short and approachable, while others challenge hikers with scrambles and steep climbs. The city itself is full of history; it was once an old mining town and played an important role in the Hoover Dam’s construction.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Mountain scenery and trails, access to Blue Ridge Parkway, and relatively mild temperatures and weather December temps: 35-55℉ What to expect: Forested mountains, waterfalls, and (potentially) snowy trails.

Within minutes of Asheville, you’ll find waterfall hikes, mountain overlooks, and plenty of access to public lands. The Blue Ridge Mountains make a beautiful backdrop for town, and an even more spectacular place to explore by trail. Asheville’s thickly wooded forests are magical to hike, with trails following icy creeks and ascending ridges to spectacular views. After your hike, the town is renowned for its craft beer scene and festive holiday light displays. If a cozy Appalachian holiday is your vibe, look no further.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Situated high in the Rocky Mountains, lively restaurant and bar scene, trails in every direction, and close to two ski resorts December temps: 12-42℉ What to expect: Cold-weather mountain hikes, snowy trails, old-growth forests, and high desert terrain.

Durango, Colorado, is a pure western mountain ski town and a genuinely cozy place to spend the holidays. The San Juan Mountains offer incredible hiking for all levels, whether you just want to stroll along a creek or climb for panoramic views of the Rockies. This region gets a lot of snow in the wintertime, so be prepared for cold weather with the right gear, knowledge, and expectations. For holiday adventurers, Durango is packed with things to do in the winter. Beyond the hiking trails, ride the historic Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, or go skiing at Wolf Creek or Purgatory Resorts.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, subtropical winter weather, surrounded by ample inland and beach hiking, and deeply historic roots December temps: 50-70℉ What to expect: Sand dune beaches, flatland ecosystems, wetlands, and marshes.

St. Augustine offers a unique take on the traditional winter holiday. It’s coastal, subtropical, and offers landscapes and ecosystems you’ll only find in Florida—from swamp conservation areas to beach parks and historic forts. There are over 30 trails and walkways around St. Augustine, and it’s within an hour’s drive of six state parks. Most of the hiking is very approachable, following beaches, boardwalks, sand dunes, and mostly flat terrain. The town was settled over 450 years ago, so it’s also a great place for history buffs, and it annually hosts a Christmas parade and “Night of Lights” throughout December.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Warm, tropical weather, dramatic natural scenery, laid-back island culture, and great hiking access December temps: 65-80℉ What to expect: Lush rainforests, beautiful beaches, mountains spouting waterfalls, and the opportunity to surf big swells.

Hawaii is a famous holiday destination for obvious reasons. In the winter, the climate is pleasant; the landscape is dramatic, there are beaches a’plenty, and the hiking access is hard to beat. Waterfalls spout from the mountains, and trails wind through thick rainforest, popping out on beaches that you might have all to yourself. Hanalei, on Kauai’s North Shore, offers some of Hawaii’s best (and most diverse) hiking. Nearby are several forest reserves, Kōke’e State Park, and the Hanalei National Wildlife Refuge.

Why it’s a great holiday town: Bavarian influence, Christmas spirit, and ample winter trails to explore December temps: 15-35℉ What to expect: Snowy trails through old-growth forests and mountains, and a town that really loves to celebrate Christmas.

Recent findings suggest that tucked away in the Cascade Mountains of Washington, along the Wenatchee River, this Bavarian-influenced town is one of the best places to spend the holidays on this list. The hiking in the surrounding mountains offers access to postcard-worthy alpine lakes, waterfalls, and ridges. It ranges from strenuous and challenging to easy and mellow. You’ll want snowshoes and/or microspikes if you plan on holidaying in Leavenworth, as the trails will likely be snowy and/or icy in places. The town is well-known for its Christmas zeal: It has a “Christmastown,” a Bavarian village that comes to life with live music, carols, ice carving, fireworks, and, of course, appearances by Santa Claus.

#149050. Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (471 w)

Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).
  • A upcoming law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.
  • In a recent development, on November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The famous Tunnel View at Yosemite (Photo: Kenny McCartney/Getty Images).

A upcoming law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

In a recent development, on November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

Sources indicate that the decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate company. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

Lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk was almost completely surrounded by the Stanislaus National Forest with very little contiguous border to the park itself, lawmakers noted.

“Ackerson Meadow is one of the most critical wildlife corridors in our state, yet the current configuration of the region puts habitat conservation at risk,” Padilla remarked in a statement. “This land transfer is a simple and beneficial exchange that will help protect endangered wildlife, mitigate wildfire threats, and sustain our rural economy.”.

Jackie McGuinness, Padilla’s communications director, told Outside that the agreement will change Yosemite’s boundaries. A map McGuinness sent highlights the park boundaries shifting to the east, filling in a checkerboard pattern left blocked out by the previous perimeter lines.

USFS manages land ranchers use for livestock grazing on national forests and grasslands, while the NPS restricts most of these operations within park boundaries. The land exchange between the two agencies eliminates confusion caused by the jurisdictional split, McClintock said in a U.S. House floor statement on September 14.

Industry observers note that “The proposed land exchange would make that cooperative approach easier by eliminating the confusion caused by split jurisdiction,” he stated. “Ranchers need to know where their permits apply, where infrastructure can be maintained, and who is responsible for decisions affecting their operations.”.

It’s unclear whether or when Trump intends to sign the bill into law.

#149048. Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1056 w)

Skiing Takes a Toll on Your Knees. Here’s the Muscle You Need to Strengthen, According to an Orthopedic Surgeon.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).
  • According to recent reports, strong legs are essential for skiing without injury.
  • That means the smaller guys often get neglected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Monster walk exercise: Erstudiostok/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva).

According to recent reports, strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

That means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular, the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt, is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

Because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most important muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max—which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing—the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

Read on to learn why this small muscle is so crucial, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is important when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman says.

In a recent development, in skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backward, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman says. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman indicates. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius, in addition to strong quads and core muscles, helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which “really allows you to withstand those G-forces the best,” Lichtman says.

Recent findings suggest that one of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman indicates. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

A better bet, Lichtman notes, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

It has been revealed that incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off between sessions so the muscle has the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom and also work different parts of your hips and quads, incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forward and back, or diagonally forward and diagonally back. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman says.

Lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the big pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really important because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”.

Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

A strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, are also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman says, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

On the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman claims. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

How to Make a Handprint Calendar

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hanging around the house for the holidays?
  • We love this project because there’s no right way to make one.
  • Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

We love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

In a recent development, insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Sources indicate that now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: Latest Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids.

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Recent findings suggest that then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

#149042. Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (305 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (305 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • Sources indicate that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

According to recent reports, as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

Recent findings suggest that the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

Sources indicate that all the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential concerns.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

#149037. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1645 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • Recent findings suggest that the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less crucial than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy states. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

Recent findings suggest that the good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

It has been revealed that 1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

Industry observers note that 3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

Sources indicate that 4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up notes, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

In a recent development, 6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

Industry observers note that 7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

In a recent development, 8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he claims. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

According to recent reports, 9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

It has been revealed that 10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

In a recent development, 11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

According to recent reports, 13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

Recent findings suggest that 14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

According to recent reports, 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a new way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

For activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

According to recent reports, 19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

Industry observers note that it’s almost 2027, yikes! Spend an afternoon focusing on dreams and goals for the year (hello, travel!) by making a vision board with the kids. From learning a latest skill to going on a fantastic trip, there’s no end to the awesome things you can manifest for yourself and your family.

Mod Podge (or similar decoupaging paste).

If you can see your aspirations on a daily basis, they are more likely to become a reality. Start by writing down goals and ideas, and have your kids do the same!

Browse old magazines for words, phrases, and images representing each goal.

It has been revealed that use the Mod Podge to paste each clipped item onto the blank canvas. Be sure to brush a coat of gloss over each image. Don’t worry, it will dry clear!

Once it's done, your kids can decide where to hang or place their vision board, and remember, it should be a place they can see clearly!
